en: The *Vinaya-śīla-mūla-ṭīkā* states that once the four pārājika offenses have been committed, one has abandoned the brahma-carya;

one falls away and descends from the noble fruits and nirvāṇa, such that there is forever no possibility of attaining them. Because they cannot be repented or removed, they are called *pārājika*. Therefore, it is said:
He said:
"If one has received the precepts but does not return them,
and while the precepts are weak, one does not relinquish them and practices the dharma of sexual desire, one commits a grave offense."
One should not engage in communal affairs with such a person.
There are nineteen matters that constitute the relinquishment of the precepts;
these are the relinquishment of the precepts, while others are not the relinquishment of the precepts.
To speak thus to the five internal groups as well as all householders and renunciants is called the forfeiture of the precepts.
Its meaning is to abandon the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, and the Pratyekabuddhas.
He abandons the study of the teachings;
he abandons communal residence and shared benefits;
he abandons the sūtras and śāstras.
I renounce my preceptor;
I renounce this bhikṣu, a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas;
you are not my bhikṣu, a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
I am a śrāmaṇera and a follower of external paths;
I am a layperson.
The superior training in ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom is called "learning."
All *poṣadha* is termed "recitation.
Dwelling together with a pure assembly that resembles a pure assembly is collectively termed "dwelling together.
Sharing the benefit of both the Dharma and material wealth is termed "sharing benefits."
The ninefold scriptures (navāṅga) are called "scriptures" (sūtra).
If one says, "I renounce the Buddhas of the past and future," this constitutes a transgression of stealing, but it is not called "renouncing the precepts.
If one speaks directly of "renouncing the Buddha," this is called "renouncing the precepts."
If one abandons the Buddha out of greed, abandons the Buddha out of attachment to external paths, or commits an offense against a Buddha, it constitutes a *steya* (theft).
If one abandons [the training] out of jest, it is a violation of the *vinaya*.

Furthermore, there are those who abandon the training, abandon the Sangha, abandon the teaching, abandon communal residence, abandon communal benefit, abandon the sūtras and śāstras, abandon the pratyekabuddhas, or abandon the upādhyāya.
As it is said in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*:
"The Dharma is nirvāṇa because it is devoid of the three time periods.
If one were to speak of relinquishing the Dharma directly [without qualification], [it would be incorrect].
If one says, "I renounce the dharmas of the three periods of time," this is called renouncing the precepts.
If one falsely says, "I renounce the dharmas of the non-Buddhists," one commits the offense of *steya* (theft). If one says, "I renounce the Ācārya," [it is likewise].
Not abandoning the precepts yet committing theft;
or saying, "I [transgress] the *āpatti-vinaya* of the past and future";
or saying, "I relinquish shared material benefits."
The same applies to renouncing many bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs.
If one falsely claims to renounce the common property and benefits with non-Buddhists, one commits the offense of theft.
If one says they are renouncing each individual bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, [the offense is as follows].
Furthermore, if one renounces [the precepts] regarding each individual monk or nun of the past or future, one violates the Vinaya.
All joking speech regarding the renunciation of the precepts constitutes a violation of the Vinaya.
However, there is no offense if it is spoken by mistake or by one whose mind is deranged.

If one intends it in the mind and speaks it with the mouth, saying "I am weak in the precepts" or "the matter of the precepts is weak," for every such utterance, one commits the offense of *steya-āpatti*.
If, having become weak [in the precepts], one does not relinquish them and engages in sexual desire,
the offense is as described above.
Second, if a bhikṣu takes an object that has not been given to him, whether in a village or in an open space—
there was a bhikṣu named Daṇḍaka who was the son of a potter;
he had previously built a grass hut which was destroyed by someone.
Later, when he made tiles that were red and beautifully adorned,
the Buddha saw them and reproached him,
ordering Ānanda to destroy them.
Later, when Ajātaśatru was guarding the city of Rājagṛha and wished to build a great mansion,
he stole five coins.
According to the law, he should have been put to death.
The King intends to pardon him.
Why would a thief die for stealing five coins?
It is because the owner cherishes them.
Therefore, the offense of one who intentionally takes [life] is grave.
For this reason, the Way of the King exhausts its legal measures;
likewise, the Tathāgata established severe prohibitions according to what was appropriate for the occasion.
In accordance with worldly affairs, things do not provoke resentment or dissatisfaction.
Although a transgression may be the same, its treatment is not uniform;
the king possesses the autonomy to adjudicate as appropriate according to the circumstances.
At times, they are subjected to extreme punishments;
at times, they are killed until their life ends;
or they are merely bound.
Some were banished beyond the borders;
some were made to pay gold as atonement for their crimes;
others were merely subjected to harsh reprimands.
These cases all concern the theft of five coins; this is the ultimate rule for their punishment.
The Buddha established these entirely based on them, in order to determine the gravity of the prohibitions regarding the objects taken.
Whether in a village or in an open space,
the village is mostly private property.
Vast tracts of land have many officials;
according to what objects belong to, they have owners.
If it is between two states and belongs to neither, it does not belong to any person.
There are those that do not belong to non-humans;
these have no owner.
If there were a Wheel-Turning Sage King in the world, [they would belong to him].
Whatever is governed by a king belongs to him;
thus, these things have an owner.
Yet, there may be things that have an owner but are not guarded or protected.
If there is no owner,
and one takes it with a thieving mind— whether it be five *kārsāpaṇas* or something worth five *kārsāpaṇas*—
the offense of stealing is committed at the moment of selection.
If one removes it from its original location, one commits a grave offense;
this applies whether the object is on the ground or in the air.
Whether located in an object or on the body,
this is called the "element of its own locus" (svadeśadhātu).
If one drags [the object] out but it has not yet crossed the boundary, one commits a grave offense of theft (*steya*);
once it has crossed these boundaries, one commits a grave offense.
This applies if it passes over the threshold of a door.
If one crosses over a horizontal object or ground of a different color,
one descends from high to low,
or ascends from low to high.
This is precisely what it means to exit the boundary.
Furthermore, when an object exists within a form,
that form constitutes the boundary.
Regarding clothing, clothing itself is the fruit;
taking an object from another's vessel,
one shifts what is above to be placed below.
If one places what is below over what is above,
one commits a grave offense in all such cases.
Furthermore, regarding theft, the intention may reside in the object itself rather than the container, or it may reside in the container rather than the object.
If both [the king and the object] are present, one commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) regarding the side where the object is located;
it is not a grave offense regarding that which is not so located. Furthermore, when one subsequently gives rise to the [intentional] mind, one again commits a grave offense.
This applies to all property belonging to the king.
A king incurs guilt by being stingy with what he has acquired;
he incurs no guilt by not being stingy when taking [what is his].
There are three kinds of taking.
Whether one takes the object oneself, instructs another to take it, or dispatches a messenger to take it,
the offense is incurred at the moment of taking.
To take an ownerless object with a thieving mind constitutes a grave theft.
If one takes five *kārsāpaṇas* belonging to a non-human being who has ownership, one commits a grave offense;
taking them from one who lacks ownership constitutes a grave theft.
Furthermore, if one intends to take five *kārsāpaṇas* from a person but mistakenly obtains four, three, two, or one, [the gravity of the offense depends on the value of what was actually taken].
A grave theft:
intending to take four, three, two, or one [units], and obtaining four, three, two, or one.
A light theft.
If one steals five *kārsāpaṇas* or more of the property of an animal, it constitutes the offense of stealing;
if it is not a precious object, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense in taking the remains of a lion's meat.
If one takes the five treasures or counterfeit treasures with the intent to steal,
whether the objects belong to sentient beings or non-sentient beings, and their value reaches five coins, it constitutes a grave offense (pārājika).
This applies even if a wild bird carries off the five treasures in its beak.
If one seizes something resembling a jewel, one commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
This is because the object should belong to the owner of the bird; thus, it is grave.
Wherever the bird follows the monk to, in each such place, one commits a grave offense.
When he steals again at another location,
and even while waiting for the birds, he steals again;
it is by the power of his incantations that he causes [the birds] to reach their respective places.
If a wild bird carries an object belonging to another,
and one seizes it when its value reaches five māsakas, it constitutes a grave theft;
this is because the bird’s mind regards the object as valuable.
Because [the value] is heavy, it is not the same as a tiger;
for the tiger’s mind does not regard it as heavy.
Even if a bird follows a bhikṣu to wherever he desires to go, it constitutes a grave offense of theft.
If one arrives at another location unexpectedly, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
likewise, if one waits for a bird, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This applies even if a wild bird seizes the property of a domestic bird.
That is, either the property of a wild bird is seized by a domestic bird,
or the property of a domestic bird [is seized by a wild bird].
The case of a bhikṣu seizing the belongings of two birds is also as explained above.
If one seizes and retains property belonging to an owner that is in the water,
one commits a grave offense (pārājika) as soon as the water reaches its destination.
Whether shifting it slightly or lifting it to move it from its original location, one commits a grave offense in all such cases.
If one makes a verbal agreement or establishes a sign such as a tree to take another's property worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, one commits a grave offense;
however, if the value is not sufficient for a grave offense, it is merely theft.
If one takes clothing or other items belonging to a teacher with a thieving mind,
it constitutes a grave offense (pārājika) when they are moved from the left hand to the right hand;
the same applies to all parts of the body.
If one uses wood, stone, or other objects to lift another object and it has already been moved from its original location,
even if it subsequently falls back to that original location, one commits a grave offense (pārājika).
If one does not pay the five-copper-coin toll at a checkpoint, it constitutes a grave offense.
If the master of the checkpoint demands a toll that should not be taken,
one must first inquire.
If taxable goods are completely brought in,
one commits an offense; if they are brought in before the deadline, there is no offense.
If one avoids taxes by taking a circuitous route, it constitutes a grave offense for stealing;
likewise, if a merchant passes goods worth five *kārsāpaṇas* through a *bhikṣu*, it is a grave offense.
Furthermore, if a merchant instructs a *bhikṣu* to pass goods [for him], it is also a grave offense.
If the time has passed or the amount is exhausted,
whether one gives the full amount or half,
or if one takes five *kārsāpaṇas* as the tax value, in all such cases one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).
If one shows the way and they pass by,
it causes the official to lose five coins as tax due to the heavy burden of theft;
furthermore, if there are robbers, wild beasts, or hunger at the frontier or mountain passes.
Whether one avoids it oneself or indicates it to another so that they may pass over it, there is no offense.
If one enters the *piṇḍapāta* (alms-food) into the Saṃgha, there is no offense;
if one does not enter it, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are ten kinds of items that do not incur a tax and for which there is no offense:
first, items belonging to the Buddha;
second, items belonging to the Dharma.
Third, the property of the Saṃgha;
fourth, the property of the upādhyāya;
fifth, the property of the various teachers.
Sixth, paternal property;
seventh, maternal property;
eighth, intending to give this property to others or to redeem one from punishment.
Ninth, it is for the purpose of returning it to its owner.
Tenth, it is for the purpose of making ritual implements,
namely, for the purpose of making the one hundred and one articles of a bhikṣu.
If one steals these ten items, one must pay the tax;
the offense for failing to pay the tax is as described above.
A bhikṣu conspires with thieves to plunder various villages.
If one obtains five *māṣaka* coins, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).
This refers to a bhikṣu who gives instructions to a village,
enabling a thief to seize the goods with ease.
There are two types of persons who steal shared property:
first, those who carry it away;
second, those who have made a prior agreement.
When carrying [the object] away, if both feet leave the ground, one commits a grave offense (pārājika).
If two people have made a prior agreement to lift it together,
this constitutes a grave offense.
If four-footed beings are lying down or tethered in one place,
whether they are taken away by force or driven out, once they have passed beyond the boundary of the four-footed area, all such acts constitute a grave offense.
If they are in a garden or walled enclosure and are driven outside, the four-footed beings commit a grave offense.
Seeing him in the grove, he thought to himself:
"I shall steal this by means of a grave theft;
if I kill him, I will fall [into hell]."
If one takes skin or flesh worth five *māṣakas*, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).
This applies even if the person is a relative, a teacher, a disciple, or a spiritual friend, provided they have been robbed by bandits or thieves and have lost their property.
If one does not give instructions for something to be taken,
and someone takes it, the taker commits a grave offense.
This applies when another person steals away one's own property.
Once one has already formed the intention to relinquish [the object], if it is subsequently seized, one commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
If one seeks to relinquish it and it is taken back, there is no offense.
If relatives have divided the property and it is in the hands of another, one must not use forceful means to seize it.
One who steals incurs a grave offense.
As for the *nāḍī* insect, one commits an offense by using it to treat swelling or weakness in the feet.
If one intends to speak of the property of the Triple Gem to another person, that constitutes a transgression.
Later, he did not commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*;
the report of his coming was grave.
Regarding the monks' meal, the Buddha did not give prior notice.
One should inform the remaining monks and the host that one is giving it to another person.
If one eats it oneself, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; furthermore, one must report this as a serious matter.
The valuable possessions of a deceased monk belong to the Saṃgha of the four directions.
If it is used as food,
or if it is divided, one commits a *duṣkṛta*;
the retribution for consuming it is grave.

If one has previously promised five coins and the intention is already settled, yet later regrets it and does not give them—even if they are kept in their original place—one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).
Furthermore, if one has previously determined to grant something to another, but does not give it even though that person has not yet requested it, one commits a grave offense.
Knowing that another has definitely consented to the theft of another's property by means of destruction, such as stealing five *kārsāpaṇas* or more,
or failing to pay a fine of five *kārsāpaṇas* at the market, which constitutes a grave offense;
or [knowing] the goods given by one who has hanged themselves.
If an official forcibly demands [an item] and one does not give it, it constitutes the offense of *sattva* (assaultive transgression).
If the value taken reaches two *kārsāpaṇas*, it constitutes the offense of minor theft (*laghu-steya*).
From two *kārsāpaṇas* up to the minimum portion that is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it constitutes serious theft (*guru-steya*).
There was a certain bhikṣuṇī who also knew that a layperson had promised to give goods to the bhikṣuṇī Yue.
He then falsely used the name of Śreṣṭhin to demand it.
The Buddha said:
"Since you obtained it, you commit an offense of false speech."
Furthermore,
it is said that one incurs an offense by falsely assuming another's name;
such an offender may commit a grave theft.
The offense incurred depends on the object to which it belongs and the quantity of that object.
If one bypasses a donor and does not accept the object, [the same applies].
If the object belongs to a householder,
one incurs an offense against that householder.
If one accepts a gift from a *vaiyyāvṛtyakara* (steward) without having given consent, [one incurs an offense].
If one gives to a non-Buddhist, one incurs an offense.
Now, regarding the giving of a layperson's gift to a non-Buddhist: a certain bhikṣuṇī gave a gift to a non-Buddhist who had previously promised to receive it from the layperson.
Because it was taken with consent, one does not commit a grave offense;
however, one incurs only the offense of speaking falsely through intentional forgetfulness.
Generally, there are seven types of taking the property of others—whether human, non-human, animate, or inanimate—in which no offense is committed.
1. The perception of it as one's own property;
2. Taking with the consent [of the owner];
3. Temporary use.
The fourth refers to one who has no master;
the fifth is one who is insane;
the sixth is one whose mind is deranged.
The seventh is the corruption of the mind by illness;
otherwise, it is a grasping.
To take another person's property constitutes a grave offense.
It is not stolen by non-humans;
it is a sudden encounter with the property of animals.
If it is an object left behind by another, it must belong to someone.
One must not take it.
If one has taken it, one must not conceal it;
it should be returned to its owner.
There is no offense in taking discarded rags (pāṃśukūla).
Generally, property belonging to the Triple Gem (triratna) should not be sold.
If one sells property belonging to the Buddha or property belonging to the Saṅgha of the four quarters (cāturdisa-saṅgha), [it constitutes an offense].
If one breaks it and takes it to another place, one incurs an offense of *thullaccaya* (grave offense) and must make restitution;
however, if it is an object intended for the mouth or an object belonging to the present Saṃgha, this does not apply.
Regarding the taking of property with full awareness, it is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If one crosses a border forgetting their slave and leaves home as an ascetic,
they commit a grave offense due to the intent to steal.
If many people send one person to take five coins, all the many people commit the grave offense of theft.
If one takes [the property], one commits a grave offense.
If two people send one person [to take it], both commit a grave offense.
If one takes the heavy property of a non-human or an animal, one commits a grave offense of theft.
Regarding light objects: if one steals them with a mind of anger, it constitutes a grave offense of theft; stealing light objects is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

Third: If a bhikṣu, with his own hand, deprives a person of life; or if he provides a weapon, instructs another to provide a weapon, instructs another to kill, or praises death—even if the person dies as a result of these actions—that bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* offense. If a bhikṣu, with his own hand, deprives a person of life; or if he provides a weapon, instructs another to kill, or praises death—even if the person dies as a result of these actions—that bhikṣu commits a *pārājika* offense.
The Buddha was staying by the Vāgvatī River.
There, the bhikṣus were practicing the meditation on impurity and became weary of the retribution of their existence.
Or [there was the case where] one wished to commit suicide;
the Brahmin Mṛgaśiras severed the lives of sixty bhikṣus with his own hands.
On account of this, the precept was established.
There are three ways of taking life:
doing it oneself, commanding another to do it, or sending a messenger to do it.
When that life is severed, the bhikṣu commits a grave offense.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of killing:
those performed by means of the body,
or those performed by means other than the body.
Or it may be used in two ways:
if one kills another, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*).
Whether death occurs immediately or not, if death results from this act, one commits a grave offense.
One does not incur a grave offense of stealing merely because of death.
If one creates a pit of fire with the intent to kill a person,
one incurs a grave offense if that person dies.
Regarding the killing of non-humans and animals, one should understand that stealing from others is a grave offense;
all such methods of killing should be known in this way.
If one falls into a pit set by a non-human as a ruse, [one must likewise recognize the gravity of the act].
If one kills a non-human, it is the offense of stealing (steya);
if one kills a human or an animal, it is all *pārājika*.
If one makes a pit for the sake of an animal...
If an animal dies, one commits a *pāyattika* offense;
if a human or a non-human dies, it is a *thullaccaya*.
If one digs a pit, it is an indeterminate (*aniyata*) offense.
To harm all living beings:
when it is a human who dies, the offense is grave;
when it is a non-human who dies, the offense is a theft.
They fall into the realm of animals.
There is no such thing as death by sudden accident.
As for those resembling humans, it refers to the initial stage of the embryo when the body-faculty and life-faculty first arise.
One whose faculties are not yet fully developed is called a "human-like being. If,
for the purpose of killing one's mother, the fetus is caused to fall and the mother dies,
one commits a grave offense.
If the fetus dies, it is a grave theft;
if both die, one commits a grave offense;
if neither dies, it is a grave theft.
Regarding the killing of a fetus:
if the fetus dies, one commits a grave offense;
if the mother dies, one commits a grave offense of theft.
If both die, one commits a grave offense;
if neither dies, it is a grave theft.
There are two ways of seeking a knife.
Whether seeking for oneself or sending others to seek,
there are three types of lamentations over death.
Those with evil precepts include virtuous persons, humans, ghosts, and sick people;
these twelve types of persons with evil disciplinary codes are called those with evil precepts.
He spoke to those who observe evil precepts, saying:
"What use is it for you to remain long in this world?
It would be better to die early than to continue committing evil."
He says to those among the seven assemblies who maintain the virtuous precepts:
"You who uphold the virtuous precepts shall be reborn in heaven after death."
"Why do you not commit suicide?
He said to the ghost:
"How can you possibly endure such suffering and affliction?"
Why not harm yourself?
Because of that, one who kills a monk commits a grave offense;
it is not because of the death itself that there is a grave offense of theft.
If one perceives a human as a non-human and takes their life, it is a grave offense of stealing life.
If one perceives a non-human as a human and cuts off their life, it is a grave offense of stealing life.
Furthermore, if one intends to cause distress rather than to kill, yet that person’s life is nonetheless cut off, it is a grave offense of stealing life.
If one intends to steal through a stratagem but has not yet departed, it is light theft;
if one has departed but has not yet arrived at the destination, it is light theft;
if one has arrived and strikes the victim but they have not yet died, it is grave theft.
If one instructs another to go by sending a messenger with a verbal command, one commits a grave offense of theft, because the intent has already been resolved.
Regarding the two precepts of killing and stealing, both self-commissioned and commissioned acts constitute grave offenses.
For the remaining two precepts, only self-commissioned acts constitute grave offenses.
If one acts according to instruction, one does not commit a grave offense.
Generally, if one does not act intentionally, one does not commit an offense, such as when Kālodāyin entered a layperson’s house and, without carefully inspecting the bed, sat down upon it,
thereby sitting on top of another's child.
The child died immediately.
In all such cases, there is no offense;
however, when sitting, one should carefully inspect the bed.
One who does not look closely commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Fourth:

if a bhikṣu, not knowing and not seeing the empty superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), claims "I have attained such [states]," even including cases of overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Fifth: if a bhikṣu, not knowing and not seeing the empty superhuman states, claims "I have such a vision," even excluding cases of overweening pride.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
At that time, the bhikṣus were observing the summer retreat on the banks of the Vāgvatī River.
It was a season of famine.
Alms-food is difficult to obtain;
for the sake of gain and offerings, they speak to one another in praise,
claiming within the superhuman states that which they have not attained as having been attained.
Because of this, the precepts were established.
The four fruits, the four paths, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, ānāpāna-smṛti, the contemplation of impurity, and so forth, are called the "dharmas that transcend the human.
To falsely claim these things when one has not seen them, has not attained them, and has not realized them is called "ignorance" (or "not knowing").
Not seeing the Four Truths is what is called "seeing.
To emerge from the mundane world is called "surpassing humans.
To demonstrate the attainment of the dharmas that surpass humans is called "attainment."
If another person understands, one commits a grave offense;
if they do not understand, it is a grave theft.
If one intends to speak or describe [the object] through expedient means, it is a light theft.
If one has finished speaking and commits a grave offense;
or if one says that the eight classes of beings, such as devas and nāgas, came to my presence and engaged in mutual dialogue,
and this is untrue— one commits a grave offense.
If one says, "I have not given rise to sexual desire regarding the precepts," and this is untrue,
it is a grave offense of stealing; if one does not understand [the gravity of the matter], it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Even down to saying that a whirlwind or an earth-dwelling spirit has come to me—
if it is untrue, if he understands [the lie], he commits a grave offense of stealing; if he does not understand,
it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one approaches non-humans or animals without their understanding, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If they understand, it is a grave theft (*steya*).
If one instructs another to speak with forgetfulness, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one tells another person to say that they have already attained the Path,
and the other person accepts these words, they commit a grave offense;
if they do not accept them, it is a grave theft.
When the former person receives the first statement, it is *dukkaṭa*;
if they then speak to another, they commit a *pācittiya*.
This applies whether they were asked or not.
That is to say, there may be someone who,
whether being investigated or not, speaks the truth for the sake of seeking purity.
To claim knowledge when one does not know is merely empty, deceptive, and forgetful speech.
The fruits of the noble ones are augmenting dharmas;
if one attains the four foundations of mindfulness, they extend upward even to the dharmas of the Peak of Existence.
Although they have attained the fruit and its characteristics have already manifested,
such that their knowledge and vision are clear and distinct,
they then claim for themselves that they have attained a superior noble fruit.
Because this involves an inflated estimation of oneself, it is called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).
Although what is said is not true, the intent behind the speech is not empty;
because the intent is not empty, one does not commit a grave offense.
Just as Maudgalyāyana grasped the signs of entering meditative absorption but did not grasp the signs of emerging from it,

To receive these five dharmas is an offense;
to speak of them as non-offenses is [an offense].
That which is constantly practiced is the Eightfold Path.
These five dharmas are what is practiced by those who are not sublime.
The Eightfold Path is the teaching of all Buddhas;
yet Devadatta regarded the Eightfold Path as wrong.
These five factors constitute it.
With diligent application of the mind, one encounters these adverse conditions and first seeks to break the Saṃgha.
The Sangha admonished him three times, but he did not desist.

This is also a theft bordering on a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

"From now on, whoever intends to cause a schism in the Saṃgha..."
One should first offer three admonitions.

There are fourteen rules regarding the fourteen types of grave theft,
as well as theft committed during the course of an admonition.
Together they form one remainder.
From this point, there is a formal ritual (karmavācanā).
After the three admonitions, the assembly gathers.
Devadatta came forward to receive the teaching on the aforementioned matters;

yet he could not be made to desist.
The World-Honored One, knowing the time was right, left the assembly and departed.
Later, when the community of monks had gathered again,
Devadatta came once more.
He himself initiated the distribution of the counting sticks (*śalākā*), proclaiming:
"Those who agree with the former [proposal], take one.
He first distributed them to assist in the chanting of harmony.
When they have separated, four people seize them;
the Saṃgha is divided into two factions.
This is called "schism in the Saṃgha."
The four matters concerning false speech and theft constitute the first great transgression. Second,
two hundred and fifty people cast lots.
The three groups of five hundred newly ordained ordinary bhikṣus took voting sticks and followed him.
As they proceeded, each group committed the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
On that day, gods and humans were thrown into chaos.
If the Eightfold Noble Path is not practiced,
the Wheel of Dharma will not turn.
While the Buddha was in the world, obstructing the turning of the Wheel of Dharma constituted a schism in the Sangha.
Now, the performance of a schismatic formal act constitutes the breaking of the Saṃgha.
After Devadatta had broken the Saṃgha,
he was admonished by an Arhatī bhikṣuṇī.
Though admonished, he would not accept [the counsel].
His anger and arrogance increased, and with his own hands he struck and killed an arhatī.
Subsequently, he shed the blood of the Buddha.
At that time, one commits the three grave offenses of parricide.
The offense of schism (saṃghabheda) cannot be expiated;
however, the breaking of the *karmavācanā* (formal monastic procedure) can be expiated.
If two groups perform separate *karmavācanā* within a single boundary (*sīmā*),
this constitutes a schism in the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda*).
This is a grave offense bordering on a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, yet it does not constitute a formal *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding a formal legal act (*karmavācanā*) performed in accordance with the Dharma,
if one intends to subvert it but does not come to listen,
this constitutes a grave offense bordering on causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
Although they have come, they do not commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
With the intention of breaking the Saṃgha, they cause strife and discord, leading the assembly to become two factions;
this is also called the grave offense of "breaking the Saṃgha" (*saṃghabheda*).

This is not a formal act (*karmavācanā*) for schism in the Saṃgha; it is simply a *duṣkṛta* offense for dispersing [the assembly] out of ignorance. It is like the peaceful practice of water mixing with milk:
water mixes with water, and milk mixes with milk.
Thus, the single flavor remains undestroyed.
If they align their minds and share the same Dharma, the assembly will have no divergent inclinations;
as a community of a single flavor, they will dwell in peace and harmony, delighting in the Path.
Therefore, it is called "peaceful and blissful conduct.
The Vinaya Master says:
"Now, even in the case of breaking the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha, there should likewise be three admonitions."
If one does not desist after three admonitions, it does not constitute an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This point, however, cannot yet be settled according to precedent.
The Vinaya Master says:
Now, regarding the schism of the *saṃgha* through formal procedure (*karmabheda*), there is no *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
Regarding the eleventh [case], "there are other monks who agree but speak differently": after Devadatta had caused a schism in the *saṃgha*, there were other virtuous monks.
Previously, he had been on intimate and harmonious terms with Kuvha and others;
thus, in private, he compassionately exhorted them—
even if many were virtuous bhikṣus.
The subsequent statement regarding "those bhikṣus who are of like mind" refers to those four individuals who were of like mind with Devadatta;
first, one, two, and three people were admonished.
This constitutes a light theft;
however, within the Saṃgha, the *karmavācanā* admonition for grave theft applies.
Those four who assist in causing a schism in the Saṃgha commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This refers to the period after the precepts have been established.
If one does not desist despite the admonitions of the Saṃgha and assists in bringing about a schism in the Saṃgha, one commits four offenses:
a pārājika (an offense involving defeat), a saṃghāvaśeṣa (an offense requiring suspension from the community), a sthūlātyaya (a grave offense), and a duṣkṛta (a minor offense that may be confessed).
The other five hundred bhikṣus committed a grave offense bordering on saṃghāvaśeṣa.
As for the nine pure bhikṣus,
Devadatta considered himself to be a Buddha.
Since one does not enter into the eight [categories of] offenses,
one should therefore renounce the intention to cause a schism in the Saṃgha and the use of divisive speech; that is,
one's intent must no longer be the same as that of Devadatta.
This is immediately different from the teachings of the virtuous assembly;
you should quickly abandon such heterodox speech.
Devadatta became a Buddha,
with four people as his assembly.
With a Buddha and an assembly, the transformation of beings was accomplished.
Because they are able to bear the Dharma, there is no offense of "transforming" (maiming) a great adversary;
however, following [such a teacher] constitutes a grave theft.
These statements by the bhikṣu and so forth are all grave thefts.
This precedes the *karmavācanā*.
Twelfth, defiling families: wherever the group of six bhikṣus, such as Aśvakapunarvasu and others, traveled, their sitting, rising, and speech all transgressed the rules of decorum.
The four categories of *sthūlātyaya* offenses encompass all manner of evils;
for one who possesses faith and devotion,
these will utterly destroy their virtuous mind.
They held the Buddha’s Dharma in contempt and no longer respected the Sangha. Then,
the Venerable Ānanda entered the village to beg for alms.
He was greatly humiliated and returned with an empty bowl; consequently,
he saw the assembly gathered together and [the monk] being expelled according to the Dharma.
To commit various kinds of unrighteous acts is called "evil conduct" (duścarita).
To destroy another's pure mind is called "defiling another's family" (kuladūṣaka).
"Driven by desire, driven by hatred, driven by fear, and driven by delusion"—
these were the words of resentment from those who had been expelled.
At that time, the six groups of bhikṣus, including the horse trainers and others, [acted accordingly].
Hearing that the great assembly was approaching,
he knew they intended to drive him away; thus,
he either fled far off or vanished like the wind.
Some welcome the assembly back to take responsibility for their offenses;
others remain at their original places of delusion, resentful as they are driven away,
claiming that their commission of evil is no different [from those who have already repented].
Departing and remaining should be treated alike;
that they are not so now must surely stem from love and hatred.
Either out of contempt for me or fear of others,
or due to the darkness of ignorance and lack of understanding,
they harbor an uneven mind.
Their conduct was unjust;
thus, out of anger and resentment, they refused to accept admonition,
continuing to commit transgressions even before being advised.
If one commits an offense belonging to another category,
when a single person, two persons, or three persons first offer individual admonition, it is a light *sthūlātyaya*;
during the formal monastic assembly, after one or two admonitions, it is a double *sthūlātyaya*.
If one does not desist after three admonitions, one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The thirteenth [offense] is being of a bad character and refusing admonition. This was due to Channa’s bad character, resentment, perversity, and pride;
he was exclusively self-willed and would not repent.
When others transgress the precepts and do not repent,
they hear admonitions and parables—
whether they be harsh or gentle.
Regarding that which is not accepted, this is called "difficult to converse with.

To be difficult to converse with is equivalent to being impossible to converse with. [The Buddha] explained the matters concerning the transgressions of the precepts, saying: "What we have spoken of as transgressions are all indeed precepts."
The matters in the Sūtras are not created by forgetfulness. "According to the Dharma" (yathādharma) means according to the principle; it is called "according to the Dharma.

"According to what is good" (yathākuśala) refers to loving-kindness and repentance, because they emerge from mutual admonition and mutual purification of offenses. Generally, when one recites the precepts, offers admonition, repents, and purifies oneself of offenses, these are the practices involved.
One must act in harmony and accord;
in principle, there should be no exclusivity or isolation.
Thus, the assembly may flourish and grow.
Therefore, you must not act with such self-will as to refuse counsel and repentance. If one does not offer admonition when it is called for up to three times,
one may sever the roots of goodness and destroy the True Dharma.

If one’s three admonitions are made with utmost sincerity, the offender will reflect and accept the penalty for themselves. Regarding the nine initial offenses (pārājika), there are four types where admonition up to the third time is permitted. Regarding the five residual offenses (saṃghāvaśeṣa), if they are committed through preparatory effort or if the act is completed, admonition is not admitted.
If one conceals their faults in secret and does not obstruct [the truth],
they may not be admonished. One should construct two large rooms and establish limits to provide necessary restraint.
In a formal act (karmavācanā), regarding a single matter, there may be both permission and prohibition.
That which is prohibited should be subject to admonition;
that which is permitted is of a different nature.
It is unlike the preceding five cases,
nor is it the same as the subsequent four. Furthermore,
the construction of a large dwelling exists for the sake of spaciousness and comfort.
The intention of leniency is not to lead one into deluded attachment,
nor is it to allow evil to reach the state of purity;
if one does not strictly and heavily restrain them, they will simply cease.
Without requiring three formal admonitions, one undergoes *parivāsa*.
In the language of Qin, this means "separate dwelling.
Once the offense has been confessed, the community grants the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and causes him to dwell separately.
While one is undergoing *parivāsa*, if visiting monks arrive from outside and one intends to confess the offense,
one should perform the *parivāsa* in such a way that it is equal in duration to the days of concealment (*tirokuṭika*).
During the day, he labored for the sake of the assembly;
at night, he stayed and slept in a separate room.
He did not begrudge these humble hardships.
He should cause the assembly to regard him with compassion.
Thereafter, he shall be granted a six-night *mānatva*.
While he is undergoing the *mānatva* to suppress and sever [the offense], if guest monks arrive, he must likewise confess.
Furthermore, day after day, he addresses the assembly, saying:
"I have committed such-and-such an offense and completed such-and-such an act.
For as many days as have passed, and for as many days as remain, he remains in a state of humiliation and subjugation.
Therefore, it is called "suppressing through abandonment.
If the sixth day is nearly complete and one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense,
yet confesses it immediately, there is no need for the period of *parivāsa*.
However, if one is further subjected to six nights of confinement and severance,
it is called "punishment for the original day" (*mūlāpakarṣa*). If,
before the period of separate residence (*parivāsa*) has been completed, one commits another offense again, [the same procedure applies].
Regarding concealment: for each day concealed, one must be granted *parivāsa* (probation) again.
If the days of subsequent concealment are fewer than the days of prior concealment, it is not necessary to grant *parivāsa* at all.
*Āpattivyutthāna* (or *ābhuhaṇa*) is termed "expiation of the offense."
When the six days have elapsed, one shall perform the *karmavācanā* before an assembly of twenty to cause [the offender] to weep and to purify them of their offense.
"Purification of the offense" (*pārivāsika*) means departing from within the offense.
For those who must undergo the period of separate residence (*parivāsa*), once four or more persons are present, they may be granted it.
This is because twenty people are required for the expiation of the offense.
As the retribution for the offense is about to conclude,
you should cause your mind to reach the great assembly.
Facing such [a situation], one's sense of shame and remorse will surely be profound.
Furthermore, having many people witness the realization of wisdom ensures that there will be no suspicion among those who come after.
Four persons, including the *nakha* (claw), may perform the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts).
The five persons perform the *pravāraṇā*.
One person performs the *pravāraṇā-karman* as the one who solicits the others.
This solicitor then receives the commission of the Saṃgha.
The other four persons state that the teacher does not receive the commission; therefore, there is the attainment of the four persons who recite the precepts.
Second, the non-empty dharmas: because Kāḷudāyin sat with a woman in a secluded place.
The laywoman Mṛgāramātṛ attained the first stage of the path.
A trustworthy person reported what he had seen to the Buddha:
"Whatever offense a bhikṣu commits is certainly subsumed within the five categories."
However, because one does not know what act, what offense, or which of the ten thousand categories of offenses it is subsumed under,
and although it is seen with certainty, it is not fixed; therefore,
it is designated by the name "indeterminate."
If a laywoman (upāsikā) bases her case on a transgression,
one may accept her testimony because she is deemed trustworthy,
yet refuse what she asserts because it has not been verified.
Furthermore, one should ask this trustworthy person:
"Do you have evidence?
He replies: "I have evidence."
Furthermore, one should inquire about the witness.
If the witness is consistent, one accepts;
if it differs, one does not accept.
Having heard the words of a trustworthy person, one should ascertain the bhikṣu who is under suspicion.
If the bhikṣu confesses the truth, he should be dealt with according to the facts;
if he does not confess the truth, the *mṛgya-karman* (act of seeking) should be performed against him.
If one has not received the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act), they shall be expelled and their offense investigated;
during this interim period, they must not serve as an *upādhyāya* or any other type of preceptor,
nor may they confer the full ordination upon monks or nuns.
Regarding the number of persons required for relying upon a teacher,
such various [requirements] cannot be obtained;
it is just as with a śrāmaṇera who has received the precepts.
Generally, a laywoman who has taken the three refuges and the five precepts is also called a person worthy of trust.
Second, regarding the case where the bhikṣu Yinli sat in the open with a woman and spoke to her: the householder Sathaha saw this and censured him.
He immediately reported this to the Buddha, saying,
"Since it is an open space, many people will see [the monk] there;
this will surely lead to censure and suspicion."
This is also not permissible;
even with one's mother or sister, it is likewise forbidden because people do not understand [the law].
The *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* states:

"The reason it is placed after the two [sections on] *pārājika* and before the three [sections on] *saṃghāvaśeṣa* is precisely because the *aniyata* offenses are lighter than those of the five [remaining] sections; thus, they are situated therein."
I consider that the preceding two sections dealt with grave offenses and have been explained to their conclusion.
Should anyone have committed such transgressions, they ought to reflect upon them with earnest attention.
Therefore, I shall now explain the section on indeterminate offenses so that they may bring them to a definitive resolution.
Regarding the thirty matters of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: one should relinquish surplus wealth;
yet because the offense leads one into the evil realms, it is called "relinquishment-and-fall" (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Regarding the forfeiture of an object for *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses, one must relinquish it in the presence of others.
Why must it be relinquished even if it is not real?
It is so that [the offender] may recognize the illegality [of their action] and give rise to a sense of shame and remorse.
Thus, the greedy mind becomes thin.
There are two kinds of relinquishment:
first, the relinquishment of giving.
Second, the relinquishment through pure giving:
impure items should be relinquished as gifts;
surplus pure items should also be relinquished as pure gifts.
The three robes, the alms bowl, and the one hundred and one items for daily use are not considered surplus;
they need not be formally relinquished as such.
All other surplus items must be formally relinquished.
If one gives impure things less than one cubit in length, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if more than that, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding cotton, thread, yarn, or three hairs, if they are discarded as refuse, it is an impure discard and a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If silk or cotton cloth has already been formally dedicated as a pure gift (*pariṣkāra*),
one need not perform a formal relinquishment (*pratyāstāra*) when making it into a robe; however,
this applies only so long as the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* robe has not yet been cut.
To trade for extra robes constitutes an offense of expiation with forfeiture; the extra robe must also be relinquished.
If one accepts [the robe] through the formal act of purification (*pariśuddhi*), and the person who relinquishes it takes the object for their own use, it is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).
One should seize [the property] by force and compel repentance.
If it is sought through hardship and not returned, the person who received the pure gift (śuddhadāna) commits a grave offense.
If it is communal property belonging to a full quorum or even many people, there is no need for a formal relinquishment of purity (śuddhiparityāga).
Pure objects such as silk cloth and the like are relinquished to a *mahābhikṣu*;
food and drink are properly relinquished to a *śrāmaṇera*;
and precious objects are relinquished to a layperson (*avadātavasana*).
Regarding the subsequent search for pure items,
the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one distributes items within the Saṃgha, each person shall receive one portion."
One must perform the ritual of "purification through consent" (saṃvāsasammuti);
if one does not do so, one commits an offense of transgression (pācittiya).
If two people obtain an object together, [the same applies].
There is no offense when [the robes] have not yet been distributed.

First, regarding the *kathina* robe: one may keep an extra robe for ten days. This applies to those obtained after the conclusion of the *varṣā* retreat or those obtained during the *kaṭhina-āstaraṇa* (the distribution of the merit-cloth).
When the ten-day period for urgent giving has concluded, one must relinquish the robe on that very day.
If the robe has already been relinquished within the first to the tenth day, there is no offense;
however, this is because the subsequent succession of days remains uninterrupted.
One who obtains [the robe] on the tenth day is one who has committed an offense; however,
there is no offense for one who washes it and keeps it beyond the tenth day,
because it reverts to its original state.
There are four cases in total.
Either it consists of the three robes or items other than the three robes;
these are all that have been used and possessed, yet have not been relinquished.
There are two types of *kaṭhina* robes:
those that are complete or those that are incomplete,
which are made complete by means of the *kaṭhina* ceremony.
This causes one to be deficient in two types of precepts.
By relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe, one becomes deficient in the three robes; there are two ways in which this relinquishment occurs.
Either it is relinquished due to the eight unfavorable conditions;
or, as some say, it is relinquished when the three [robes] are complete;
or, even when the three robes are complete, one relinquishes the *kaṭhina* robe.
The *kaṭhina* robe should be designated as having one share of the benefit;
the remaining *kaṭhina* benefits are said to be "sufficiently relinquished.
If there are fewer than two [robes], or if the three robes are absent.
One does not obtain the *guṇa-cīvara*.
Or, if one is lacking even three robes and has not relinquished the *guṇa-cīvara*,
this refers to one who has already obtained it.
If one has not yet requested the small items required to complete the robe, it is called "incomplete.
Among the merits, there are seven benefits obtained through relinquishment.
The seven precepts are without fault.
At the conclusion of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), if there is no *kāṭhina* robe,
one must not stay overnight separated from the three robes.
Furthermore, during the one-month period, one also obtains five benefits:
namely, eating repeatedly; entering a village before the meal and entering a village after the meal;
and departing without having announced one's intention.
Regarding the keeping of surplus wealth and eating separately from the community, one need not inform others before eating; however, the *kaṭhina* robe is excluded.
The differences lie in the distribution of robes during the rainy season retreat and staying apart from one's robes overnight.
Therefore, monks who sit later [in the assembly] do not obtain this day.
Once the regulations have been established, the summer retreat has passed and one enters the winter season;
for during the summer, there is much traveling to pay respects at stupas and to attend upon teachers and elders.
Because the donor’s heart was joyful,
the Buddha permitted that the objects of offering be purified beforehand;
once the initial *kaṭhina* robe ceremony is completed, they are no longer purified by such an act.
Second, one must not stay overnight separated from the three robes. To distinguish themselves from non-Buddhists, the cutting of the robes (khaṇḍa-cīvara) was permitted;
for the sake of cold weather, the three robes were permitted;
and the outer robe (saṃghāṭī) is to be worn when entering a village.
The upper robe (antaravāsaka) is for entering the assembly;
the lower robe (nivasana) is for private use.
If one lacks the *kaṭhina* robe or has already relinquished it, it constitutes being separated from one's robes.
They were lost during the latter part of the night.
Later, because Śāriputra was elderly and his robes were heavy,
the Buddha permitted the assembly to perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to retain them.
Generally, when one grows old, their robes become heavy;
since the time of Upagupta, there has been no *kaṭhina* robe.
On the ninth day of the month, he went out wandering at midday.
Regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*), if one becomes heavy with them, the community may perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the relinquishment of one robe; thus, there is no offense.
The third category, the seasonal robe (*kālacīvaram*), was established because the group of six bhikṣus (*ṣaḍvargika*) were insatiable in their greed and seeking.
When one obtains robes during the period of the *kaṭhina* robe, they are called "timely robes" (*kālika-cīvara*).
There is no offense in keeping such timely robes for an extended period.
Once the *kaṭhina* period has ended, they are called "untimely robes" (*akālika-cīvara*).
Receiving objects with one's own hands clarifies what is not permitted;
gold, silver, and other impure items must not be accepted. If a robe is damaged, it may be repaired;
if a cat’s paw has caused a loss, it should be promptly restored.
However, if one receives [the robe] again after having returned it, there is no *naissargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture); one incurs only a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If it is made up on the same day and not until many days later, there is no offense for receiving it even for a brief moment due to the circumstances.

The same applies when the edge or the seam of a robe is torn. If the indefinite *guṇa-cīvara* (extra robe) has not been completed, even if one’s three robes are sufficient, one may keep extra wealth for ten days.
However, if the three robes are incomplete and one obtains cloth of various colors...
If the individual pieces are not yet sufficient to make a robe,
it is permitted to keep them for one month.
Once the month has passed, they must be joined together.
If garments made of various colors are joined together but still fall short, one may be permitted to seek more to make them sufficient.
Once they are sufficient, there is no fixed limit to how many are made.
If one kind of cloth or a single color of cloth is insufficient,
one may make it while seeking what is sufficient,
provided it does not exceed one month.
If one intentionally does not seek [the robe] and it is not limited by days or months,
yet knows there is another place where it can be obtained for the purpose of making up the deficiency, one should know that this refers to a place of a great assembly.
If one personally manages the household, one should obtain more;
for the sake of serving [the recipient], one should supplement it so that it becomes sufficient.
One may keep it for one month as an impure gift (*aśuddha-dāna*).
The remaining materials are not used for making robes;
they are like the normally pure gift-robes (*śuddhaka-cīvara*),
which must be at least two and a half cubits in size for the three robes (*tricīvara*).
If the measurement of the *khaṇḍa* (hem) is like that of the *nivāsana* (lower robe), one may receive it as a lower-grade garment to serve as one of the three robes (*tricīvara*).
Fourth, receiving a robe from a nun who is not a relative: when the bhikṣuṇī Puṣpavarṇā offered meat to the assembly, she was wearing only a single robe.
The robes were of the highest quality.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw them, they coveted them,
and the nun immediately gave them to them.
He himself wore tattered robes.
The World-Honored One questioned him with wonder,
and because of this, the precept was established.
For three reasons, the taking of a nun’s robe is prohibited:
first, because it is difficult for a nun to obtain robes;
second, because taking them from one who is not a relative lacks propriety.
Third, because there is the fear that subsequent thoughts might give rise to what is not the Dharma,
it is permitted to exchange [goods] according to one's own preference.
If one possesses money or silk worth *kārṣāpaṇa* or more, one may trade for them.
If one does not exchange the three robes with the *saṃgha*, for a *nirvāṇa-saṃgha* (monastic robe),
from the *kaṣāya* upward, it is an offense of falling (*pāyattika*);
below that, it is a minor offense (*dukkaṭa*).
It is also an offense to exchange debt for goods.
If many bhikṣus take a single robe from one bhikṣuṇī, many people commit an offense.
When taking from many bhikṣuṇīs, the offense is incurred according to the number of bhikṣuṇīs involved.
As for the nun who has left the household life, because she has not yet received the *śrāmaṇerī* precepts,
there are five places to which she should not go;
namely, those of the unmarried girls (*mahā-kumārī*).
A woman whose husband has been granted a pardon; a prostitute;

namely, clarified butter, oil, honey, and rock sugar.
The bhikṣu Nakṣatra stored various medicines in large quantities,
allowing them to remain for several nights;
because of this, the rule was subsequently relaxed.
If one is ill, it is permitted to take the four kinds of compound digestive medicines;
they should be discontinued once the illness has been cured.
If there is no attendant (kappiyakāraka) to whom they may be entrusted, [one may take them oneself].

and may be consumed for seven days.

if they have not yet been formally accepted by mouth or received by hand,

Throughout one's life, one should receive and consume [the substances] from a *naiṣadyika* (attendant) every day.
One should receive and consume the *kālika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the specific time) at the appropriate time.
As for the *yāmika-bhaiṣajya* (medicines for the watch of the night), if one receives them with one's own hand, they need not be received by verbal formula.
If time has passed, one must receive it again.

One may take and consume it oneself during the seven days; however,
if one has not received it by mouth or by hand,
one should receive it daily from a *kappiya-kāraka* (an attendant).
Regarding lifelong medicine, it may be received by hand or received by word;
one may take it oneself for life.
If it is received by hand but not received by word, [it is likewise permissible].
Therefore, one receives it daily from a *kappiyakāraka* (a person who renders things permissible).
If one does not receive it by mouth or by hand, having performed the ritual of purification and relinquishment (*visajjana*), [it becomes permissible].
For the rest of one's life, one should receive clothing from a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites).
This is for the purpose of preventing thoughts of theft.
All food and drink must likewise be received from a *kappiya-kāraka*.
A person who is not ill may not receive seven-day medicine by mouth; however,
if a sick person receives it by mouth or receives it with the hand,
the medicine has not yet passed overnight.
One who is not ill may take [the medicine].

Regarding the fortnightly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*): if the fortnightly recitation of the precepts is not performed, there is an offense of transgression (*duṣkṛta*).

The first instance of false speech: There was a bhikṣu named Khāḍi, who was intelligent and fond of debate.
A brahmin came wishing to engage him in a contest of arguments.
Aṅgada was afraid of him and,
speaking deceitfully,
said that he had gone out for alms and would not return.
An evil reputation spread abroad;
consequently, the precept was established:
one must not speak falsely.
False speech subsumes four categories and five types of precepts.
To claim superhuman attainments through false speech constitutes a grave offense;
it is a case of speaking without discernment.
To speak and then retreat into concealment constitutes an offense of *steya* (theft).
To slander another with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
To falsely accuse another of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) offense.

To falsely accuse another of an offense constitutes a *pārājika* (defeat). To claim knowledge of what one has seen, heard, or cognized when one suspects it is false— namely, when one has not actually seen,
heard, or cognized it— is likewise [a grave offense].
If one does not see, hear, know, or perceive something, yet falsely claims to have seen, heard, known, or perceived it—
this false claim, arising from greed, hatred, or delusion, is entirely termed "knowing and speaking falsely," which constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika).
Therefore, it is known that one speaks falsely.
"Speaking with the nails" is distinct from "knowing.
All instances of speaking falsely while knowing constitute an offense of *pāyattika*.
The second is harsh speech. There are four types of clans:
first, the royal lineage from the beginning of the kalpa;
second, the brāhmaṇas.
In the beginning, they were practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The third [class] is the Vaiśyas;
the noble clans and those of intermediate caste are always referred to in advance as *gṛhapati* (householders).
The fourth is the śūdra,
the lowest mixed caste.
These four types of people may leave the household life and receive the precepts.
The group of six, out of malice and resentment, uttered eight kinds of insults.
These eight kinds are: [insults regarding] caste, occupation, transgressions, illnesses, physical appearance, afflictions, verbal abuse, and [insults regarding] the three preceding castes.
They spoke thus to those of the three castes.
For one of such a lineage, what is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?
Because of a mind of contempt, each word constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
for one of lower mixed caste, each word constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Because their sense of shame was profound, he spoke to those of the three preceding castes, saying:
"You should practice the arts as is appropriate;
what use is it for you to leave the household life and receive the precepts?"
For each individual word, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For each word spoken to one of the mixed castes, it is an offense of *pācittiya*.
Having understood [the rule], if one speaks again after having already explained it, it is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one does not understand the offense,
one says to four kinds of people:
"You have committed an offense against the last four categories of precepts."
Such are the signs of a malignant disease;
such are the heavy afflictions;
and such are these two kinds of people who revile others with evil words.
"What is the use of leaving home and receiving the precepts?
Furthermore, you compose works both for those who have left home and for those who remain at home to revile the Dharma, disparaging it."
Regarding those four castes, if one disparages each of them or commits each of the offenses, it constitutes a *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, if one disparages a great bhikṣu by means of any matter other than these eight, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one disparages a śrāmaṇera, a layperson (*avadātavasana*), a non-human, or an animal by means of these eight matters, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa*.
If one reviles in accordance with reality,
it is a case of reviling that is not false speech;
one reviles, yet it is not untrue.
This is slanderous and false speech.
Third is divisive speech: although the wickedness of divisive speech may be reconciled by kindness, the Six Groups of Monks act with unrestrained license and commit such acts without shame.
To speak emptily and without basis,
inciting conflict between this and that,
so that both sides are troubled and disturbed.
They themselves lose their own practice; they exhaust their bodies, yet later claim credit for their efforts and speak with flattery.
Their actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely unwholesome, as they incite other bhikṣus to create a schism into two factions.
Desiring to sell [the offense] in two places and intending to provide divergent accounts to both sides,
he spoke to the renunciants of the three aforementioned castes,
saying: "A certain name, a certain surname, suffering from a certain illness, performing a certain act, and having a certain appearance."
The bhikṣu said,
"If you cultivate in such a manner,
what is the use of leaving the household life and receiving the precepts?"
Whether for the sake of explaining or not explaining,
once explained, he speaks of each offense one by one.
The same applies to the performance of crafts.
Regarding the mention of various castes:
if one explains it and then speaks further,
for each instance of speaking after having explained, the offender commits a *pāyattika* offense.
Not understanding the offense;
performing artistic crafts in the same manner;
subsequently committing an offense; being afflicted by illness; and reviling others—these five matters constitute the act of double-tongued speech.
The bhikṣus of the four castes understood this;
having understood it, they spoke further.
For each word spoken after understanding, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not understand [the offense], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Furthermore, if one causes a separation from a *mahābhikṣu* by means of other matters, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one separates any other person or non-human being by means of the eight matters, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
The fourth monastic matter concerns the re-initiation of what had been suspended: The bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were of evil character and prone to anger;
their quarrels did not cease.
The World-Honored One departed from there and went to Śrāvastī.
The elders and householders all grew resentful and reproached him;
the bhikṣu was filled with shame and fear,
and he followed the Buddha to seek repentance.
Once the assembly had reached a verdict and they had been reconciled,
the group of six bhikṣus instructed them to gather again and incite a dispute.
The first category, "contention through speech," subsumes all the following types of contention;
within this, it is further divided into the latter three.
2. Disputes concerning groundless slander;
3. Disputes concerning matters of violating the precepts;
4. Disputes concerning customary practices.
This refers to the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*),
all formal acts of the Saṃgha (*karmavācanā*), and the occasions when disputes arise during various monastic affairs.
There are five kinds of bhikṣus in total.
First, the resident bhikṣu;
second, the visiting bhikṣu;
third, the bhikṣu who has been entrusted with the matter.
There are monks who commit offenses and monks who hold views;
these types of monks give rise to four kinds of disputes.
The assembly shall extinguish it according to the Dharma by means of seven matters. If,

or if doubt regarding the extinction arises again, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one perceives an illegal extinction as a legal extinction,

If the characteristics of what is illegal arise again as characteristics of what is illegal, there is no offense.
The fifth [offense] is preaching the Dharma to women in excess of five or six words. Kāḷudāyin’s fire of lust was blazing intensely;
since the precepts for the two categories had already been established, he was not permitted to do otherwise.
Through speech, he disperses their entanglements of affliction;
he delights in describing the physical characteristics of women in various ways,
or speaks of his own mother to women.
Or, she might tell her mother about the girl.
Because of the spread of such ill repute,
this rule was established.
There are women who must not be taught.
To explain that "form is impermanent" constitutes one sentence;
by the time one reaches "consciousness is impermanent," it constitutes five sentences.
If one speaks of the six sense bases as being six categories,
yet speaks without having been asked, one may not exceed five;
if one exceeds the five or six words, for every such word, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one recites verses, recites chapters, or recites sūtras, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
Fearing that this might lead to the arising of what is not Dharma through the Dharma,
these limits were established to prevent it.
If one were to say nothing at all, there is a fear that they might give rise to thoughts of inferiority;
therefore, it is appropriate to speak briefly so that they may attain respectful faith.
If a woman asks about the Dharma herself, one may answer her according to her questions.
Furthermore, it is permissible to bestow the three refuges, the five precepts, or the eight precepts; likewise,
there is no offense in chanting, offering prayers of aspiration, or praising and explaining the merit of giving,
provided that a knowledgeable man is present.
This refers to a layperson who is able to discern good from evil;
a wise woman is likewise.
One must not speak [of such matters] with a great bhikṣu or a śrāmaṇera as companions.
To speak [of this] is a *dukkaṭa* offense.

Sixth, one may teach those who have not received full ordination using *cāndāla* verses; *cāndāla* refers to the script of the Brahmins.
The meaning, flavor, verses, and phrases differ from those of the Buddha’s sūtras.
Furthermore, they instruct the Buddha’s disciples to recite in unison;
because they follow the sound of the voice, the meaning and flavor become incorrect and improper.
The verses are incomplete.
A bhikṣu from the country of Ālambīya was the son of a brāhmaṇa.
When teaching those who have not yet received the precepts,
one uses their own original method of chanting by blending the sounds together;
because this follows the mere sound, the name and flavor are incorrect.
Deficient in verses and gāthās,
they defame the True Dharma and increase their evil habits.
Such an instruction is not permitted by the Buddha.
If one instructs a śrāmaṇera to commit the same offense as a layperson, it constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
This is because their practice of the Dharma has not yet become deep.
Because they follow what is deviant and profound;
furthermore, because their subtle sounds and confused speech make them indistinct,
those who possess the complete precepts commit an offense.
Because his mind is already resolved and unshakable,
and because the sounds are similar and not confused,
he instructs those who have not yet received full ordination.
If one utters the sounds of non-Buddhists (tīrthika) with complete or incomplete phrasing and meaning, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one wishes to abandon the original sound but cannot achieve [the correct pronunciation], there is no offense.
If one uses the sounds of the Dharma, complete in both name and meaning, there is no offense.
There is no offense if two people recite together a sutra that one has previously memorized.
The Vinaya Master says:
"Once finished, it is finished."
This refers to two people who were originally both non-Buddhists;
they recited a single sutra together,
yet one forgot it while the other completed its recitation.
Thereafter, one person recited again without transgression.
Furthermore, both the teacher and the disciple were originally followers of external paths;
the disciple who had received the Dharma did not yet understand the words of the Dharma.
To receive and recite [the teachings] by matching the sounds is called *uddeśa*.
Furthermore, if a disciple acts as a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*),
the teacher may respond to their questions accordingly without offense.
If one utters these words together with another, both commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Seventh: To speak of one's own superhuman attainments (*uttarimanussadhamma*) in the presence of a person who has not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
One should disclose what is evil and conceal what is meritorious.
Regarding the limit of the *mākauha* (the offense of false claim):
it refers to a bhikṣu who, before others, claims for himself what he has not attained.
This constitutes the first *pārājika*, as already explained.
If one truly commits this offense of falling (pāyattika) while claiming it oneself,
śrāmaṇeras and laypeople— being flighty, unstable,
and prone to forgetfulness— will spread [the news].
It is difficult to speak the truth.
Furthermore, if one seeks fame and profit among laypeople,
speaking the truth to them would constitute a violation of this precept in both cases.
To speak of the four paths, dhyāna, samādhi, ānāpāna, or the contemplation of impurity, and to tell others that devas, nāgas,
and the eight classes of beings have all committed a *pārājika* offense, is a transgression. Likewise,
if one truly maintains the precepts but speaks of them to others [in such a manner], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one sees a whirlwind or an earth-demon (*pṛthivī-devatā*) and speaks of it to another person, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, there is no offense in speaking to one who has received the Dharma, a meditation master (*dhyāna-ācārya*), or one who possesses the precepts and shares the same intent.

Eighth: If a bhikṣu knows of a grave offense and speaks of it to a person who has not yet received full ordination, he commits a *pāyattika* offense, except in the case of a formal monastic act (*saṃgha-karman*). All offenses among the five categories of transgressions are termed "grave" (*pāpaka*).
With the exception of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, all others are termed persons who have not received the full ordination (anupasaṃpanna).
To speak of another’s transgression of the precepts to such a person—
referring to offenses of the first two categories— is called the offense of falling (pāyattika).
To speak of the actual act constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding the three final categories [of the Prātimokṣa], to state the name of the offense while stating the facts constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases,
except when it concerns a formal monastic procedure (*saṃghakarma*).
If a bhikṣu commits an evil transgression against the householders and causes them to feel resentment,
the Saṃgha present there should act in harmony and appoint one person.
There is a bhikṣu endowed with five virtues who has performed the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* against him;
now we shall go before that lay devotee and proclaim his faults.
One should speak of the evil deeds committed by an evil bhikṣu and the misdeeds he has performed.
If one speaks of them in another place or to another person, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This applies once the formal act of proclaiming the offense (*āpattipratijñākarma*) has been completed.
When that wicked bhikṣu becomes increasingly malevolent and causes affliction to the Saṃgha,
a formal motion followed by three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) should be performed,
directing the entire Saṃgha to follow him to the place where he commits his evil deeds.
One may speak of their faults at will and at any time;
however, one must not speak of the offenses categorized under the five groups of rules.
If one speaks of them, it shall be considered a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Other monks who have not performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā) may not speak of the faults of others under any circumstances.
There are five types of cases in which one may speak of another's faults.
First, regarding the five categories of offenses (pañcāpatti):
If one sees [an offense] but has the perception of seeing it while lacking the perception of not seeing it,
the same applies to the perception of doubt regarding what was heard.
Second, if one sees another commit an offense of the first category (pārājika).
Some say he has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
some say he has committed an offense belonging to the last three categories.
The same applies to the remaining four categories.
If, when speaking, one speaks again of the original name and the original matter;
thirdly, seeing another commit a primary offense (āpatti),
one gives rise to doubt as to whether it constitutes a pārājika.
The same applies to the other four categories [of offenses] besides the *pārājika*.
Later, having resolved his doubts, he spoke again of the original name and the primary matter.
Fourth, he saw another commit a primary offense.
If one suspects that another has committed an offense belonging to the other four categories,
and likewise sees another commit such an offense while remaining in doubt,
then once the doubt is subsequently severed, one should state the original name and the specific facts of the case.
Fifth, seeing another commit an offense of the first category (pārājika),
