if there are many monks and many nuns, it is a *pāyattika* for each monk;
if there is one monk, it is one *pāyattika*.
If there are many monks or two nuns, it is likewise a *pāyattika* for each individual monk.
If one still remains in an open space of five hundred bow-lengths, one commits a *pāyattika*;
if one turns back midway, it is likewise.
If one does not intend [to cross] but simply passes through directly, there is no offense.
If one is swept away by wind-blown timber and fails to reach safety,
or if the front bank collapses.
If one loses the requisites for practice, there is no offense whatsoever regarding the upper or lower robes.
Twenty-six: Giving robes to a nun who is not a relative—previously prohibited from taking them, now prohibited from giving them.
There was a bhikṣu who came from a place where robes were improperly kept;
Sūlaṇī saw him and questioned him.
He asked him for his robe;
the bhikṣu immediately gave it to him. Having given him the robe, he himself wore tattered clothes.
The Buddha said,
"If they had been relatives, one ought to have known whether or not there was anything [left behind].
Because they were not relatives, they simply took it and departed."
Furthermore, fearing that this might give rise to various forms of unrighteousness,
he did not permit [the giving of robes] to those who are not kin.
To give a robe to one who is not considered a relative, or to one whom one regards as a member of the other six groups of renunciants, constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika).
If one gives clothing to those who are neither relatives nor members of the other six groups, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This applies whether they are actually relatives or non-relatives,
or if one says they are such, or if one gives impure clothing while either certain of it or suspecting it.
This refers to garments made of camel hair, ox hair, or the wool of black sheep, as well as garments woven from a mixture of these fibers.
To give such garments [as a formal gift] constitutes an offense (dukkaṭa),
because they are not suitable for formal acceptance and are not considered valuable items.
27. Making robes for a nun who is not a relative: Kālodāyin made a robe for the nun Khujjuttarā, and he depicted a scene of male and female union upon the central panel.
Gupta came; [the Buddha] took a rolled scroll and gave it to him,
not permitting him to unroll and examine it.
Kṣudrapāla brought it back and spread it out among the bhikṣuṇīs.
The community of nuns criticized and disparaged this,

it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) because it is not in accordance with the Dharma and unfit for use.

Because of this, the precept was established:
when lustful thoughts arise uncontrollably,
one must not discriminate between those who are close and those who are distant.
Since the arising of derision and slander is likewise without discrimination, they are all severed.
One sitting constitutes one downfall;

the laypeople criticized and disparaged him.

For each instance of sitting down again after rising, one commits that many *pāyattika* offenses.

If one goes two *zhang* five *chi* away, it is an offense of a *dukkaṭa*.
If one goes three *zhang* or more than three *zhang*, there is no offense.

Regarding the thirty offenses of *pāyattika* for obtaining food through the cause of a nun’s praise: excepting the time when she was formerly a laywoman, or when there is a specific cause—such as when the four great *śrāvakas*, including Kāśyapa, accepted an invitation from a householder.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was previously in that house,
where she praised Devadatta and disparaged Kāśyapa.
When Kāśyapa heard the sound, he returned and praised her;
however, the lay couple drove her away.
On account of this, the precept was established.
It is not permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to praise food and then accept it. However,
if she has previously received an invitation,
there is no offense if she accepts it after praising it later.
If one praises [the donor] for the sake of obtaining food, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
Later, there was a householder who invited a bhikṣu;
after the meal, he went out briefly to see an acquaintance.
The bhikṣuṇīs went out to meet them;
however, because the precept had been established, the bhikṣus did not go.
When the lay devotees returned, the time for the meal had already passed.
The bhikṣu lost the food,
and the householder was deeply resentful;
because of this, it was again permitted as an exception.
First, one should be friendly.
If one is already friendly before eating, and the food was not obtained through a nun,
but the nun later praises it, there is no offense in accepting it.
If a donor first invites a nun and,
finding the food unpalatable,
urges her to prepare a more delicious meal.
To eat [such food] constitutes an offense of falling (pācittiya).
Even if a nun instructs one to put a small amount of ginger into the food,
to eat it constitutes an offense of transgression (dukkaṭa).
Thirty-first: Eating repeatedly except on account of a specific cause. The "specific causes" are: being ill, or the time for the distribution of robes.
There was once the son of a householder whose parents had passed away and whose wealth and property were also exhausted.
Desiring to perform meritorious deeds so as to be reborn in the second heaven,
he lacked the means to cultivate merit and thus worked as a hired laborer for others.
Having earned wealth through this labor, he used it to provide offerings of food for the assembly of monks.
On one occasion, the monk Jie said, "I have accepted many offerings of cakes and meat;
yet although I accepted these invitations, I have eaten very little.
The donors were distressed by this.

On festival days as well, he ate only parched grain,
consuming very little;
the ministers disapproved and rebuked him.
Because he had brought shame upon the Sangha,
this rule was established:
one must not eat more than once a day.
"Eating frequently" means eating at different locations;
this is because it leads to excessive attachment and because such food is difficult to digest.
Because it obstructs the path of practice;
because it is the dharma of non-Buddhists;
and because it is like that of a child.

If a full day has passed and one is invited to a place, one should accept the offering as a single meal from that donor.

Later, when the bhikṣus became emaciated due to illness,
a special allowance was made for the sick, permitting them to eat several times a day.
This applied to those suffering from the three types of diseases treated by hot wind therapy.
If one obtains three kinds of fine food— excellent in color, fragrance, and flavor—
one may accept an invitation for a single meal;
likewise for a second, third, or even a fourth invitation.
When three or four mouthfuls were insufficient for him to eat further, it was mid-afternoon;
at that time, various elders had prepared a meal specifically to offer robes.
The Buddha, considering that robes are difficult to obtain, wished to cause them to accept the robes.
One may accept food based on the number of robes;
if one accepts an invitation for robes while being without robes,
it shall be distinguished as follows.
Sometimes both families may invite him at the same time; when invited by one,
there is clothing and food, and when invited by the other,
there is likewise clothing and food.
The bhikṣu is without fault.
It may happen that two families invite him,
and at the time of the invitation, both provide food and clothing.
At the time of eating, there is none.
When a bhikṣu accepts an invitation, he does not commit an offense;
at the time of eating, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If both families have provided both food and clothing when the invitation was issued,
but at the time of eating one family has food while the other lacks clothing,
there is no offense for accepting the invitation in either case.
If one eats without wearing the edge of the robe, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
Or, there may be an invitation from two families;
at the time of the invitation as well as at the time of eating, one has no robe.
When a bhikṣu accepts [the food], he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense;
when he eats it, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
Or, when invited by two families, he has no robe.
If one possesses clothing at the time of eating,
the bhikṣu commits a *duṣkṛta* offense when accepting the invitation,
but there is no offense at the time of eating.
If both families have no robes when they extend the invitation,
but one has a robe while the other has none at the time of the meal,
the bhikṣu incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for accepting the invitation in both cases.
If one lacks a robe at the time of eating, it constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika).
Alternatively, when invited by both families, one possesses a robe for both;
however, at the time of eating, one lacks a robe for one of them.
When a bhikṣu accepts an invitation from one who is not wearing robes, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
at the time of eating, he commits a *pāyattika*.
Or, he may be invited by both families.
When receiving the invitation, one has no robe;
at the time of eating, both [robes] are present.
At the time of receiving the invitation, there is an offense of *duṣkṛta* regarding the absence of a robe.
There is no offense in either case when eating.
Or, both families may extend an invitation;
at the time of the invitation, one family provides clothing while the other does not.
When eating, both [the donor and the monk] have robes.
If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation while lacking a robe, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense;
when eating, if both lack robes, there is no offense.
If there are many invitations for both food and clothing,
and at the time of each meal invitation there is clothing provided,
the bhikṣu commits no offense whatsoever.
Later, when the elders gathered on festival days,
they troubled the bhikṣus; consequently,
[the Buddha] permitted them to eat repeatedly on festival days.
Some people provide food to seek merit because they perceive signs of good or bad fortune;
some provide food out of respect for those of virtuous character;
and some do so on auspicious days.
Or one may provide offerings of food on the auspicious days at the beginning of the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight;
or it may be the regular meal for the assembly.
Or they may eat in separate rooms;
or there may be invitations for the entire assembly or invitations for individuals.
On all festival days, the elders have not yet been invited.
Regarding the aforementioned invitations to eat, one should always give them to others;
yet, because one accepts those invitations,
it is said that after having given them to others, one subsequently partakes of the midday meal from among them.

If one belongs to the five groups of the ordained, one should not give away one's various alms-foods to others, because it is difficult to perform meritorious acts with food that has not been properly accumulated.
Regarding the thirty-two types of giving: in a single location, a healthy bhikṣu should take only one meal; and there is the "equal giving" where a donor builds a dwelling in a secluded place.
Providing seats, bedding, food, and drink—
bestowing all such offerings without limit—
is what is called a "house of merit."
At that time, there was a great famine and food and drink were difficult to obtain.
The group of six monks arrived at this house;
having received food and drink, they did not hear of leaving again.
Furthermore, there was another person who came seeking a place to stay.
The six groups of monks were violent and aggressive;
because of them, the host wished for the newcomer to leave.
Yet they did not dare to dispatch them.
The World-Honored One, knowing this,
established a precept on account of it.
One is not permitted to receive many [offerings].
In this house, one may stay for one night and take one meal;
therefore, it is called a "place of eating."
If one eats beyond the single meal, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If, after having passed the single meal, one stays overnight at this location and does not eat, one commits a *dukkaṭa* offense.
One ought to stay overnight at this location.
One should eat at this place.
Because one stayed overnight at this place and then ate,
one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one eats at this place and also stays overnight here, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one eats twice and stays overnight twice, one commits two *pāyattika* offenses.
Later, Śāriputra, while traveling due to illness, arrived at this house.
Because the precepts were established, they did not dare to accept [offerings] beyond the limit;
it was on this account that the allowance for illness was opened. In cases of illness, one may act according to one's own inclination.
If it is in one of the eight difficult circumstances,
or if one fears for oneself beforehand,
or if it concerns a close relative.
If one wishes to enter a dangerous path and stays therein to wait for companions,
there is no offense provided that one has great merit and stays as a resident of a dwelling of merit.
If one goes to the home of a layperson during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and is offered cakes or roasted flour, one may accept two or three bowls.
Having accepted them, one should go outside and give them to other virtuous bhikṣus.
In the Hu (Central Asian) manuscript, the word "good" (善) is absent from the middle.
A Brahmin woman, having gone out to marry and returning briefly to her home, was making cakes and parched grain flour.
She intended to send them back, but she stumbled and fell.
Nanda knew that his three or four disciples had all begged for and taken [the food],
and so he requested it three times in succession until it was completely exhausted.
His husband grumbled about the delay, cut off the lamp's wick, and went on to the next watch of the night.
At that time, he rebuked him but did not yet lay down a formal precept.
Furthermore, on another occasion, when an auspicious star appeared and the day arrived for the merchants' expected arrival.
They agreed to gather treasures together.
One merchant, Pāṇḍaka, took all the flour for himself;
he lost his companions, was plundered, and was killed by bandits.
Because the precept was established based on two conditions,
it is said:
"Whether it be cakes or parched grain, there are three kinds of bowls."
It is permitted to eat while holding the bowl;
one part broth and two parts rice,
with the upper bowl being three *sheng*.
The medium bowl holds two sheng;
the small bowl holds one sheng.
By this, such illegal practices are extinguished.
According to the laws of the land of India, a portion is set aside for beggars,
consisting of either three or four *śē* (measures).
Therefore, the Buddha permitted taking one portion from the alms bowl.
Two are taken from the middle bowl and three from the lower bowl; therefore,
it is said, "two or three bowls."
This refers to two or three people begging for alms together;
therefore, this serves as the limit.
To exceed this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
One should take it and, having measured its length, give it to another bhikṣu;
furthermore, one must measure whether the owner possesses [the requisite] or not to determine [the allowance].
If one exceeds this limit, one falls into an offense.
If someone later arrives and requests it, you should give it to them from outside [the storehouse].
If you do not distribute it, you should say:
"I have already taken this much for the donor."
If there is that much remaining,
and if you take it all, you should say:
"I have taken it all."
"You must not enter again.
If you do not divide [the space] and do not speak, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If you have already spoken previously, yet another person still enters..."
If one enters [the area], one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is not long and is not divided, there is no offense;
one should simply inform those behind so that they may know.
The Vinaya states:
"The upper bowl has a capacity of three *sheng*;
it may receive one *sheng* of rice, half a *sheng* of soup, and the remainder may be other edible foods."
The Vinaya master, however, says:
"The bowl has a formal capacity of three *śōng*;
when filled with rice, it can still accommodate soup and other foods."
Therefore, the medium and small bowls should also be understood in this same way.
Thirty-fourth: eating while not following the rule for leftover food constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika). Kālodayin was a son of the Śākyas.
His physical form was extraordinary,
and his complexion was like that of a lotus flower.
Later, he was bitten by a venomous snake.
His complexion turned black;
his eyes were red and his teeth were white.
He went out at night to beg for alms.
A flash of lightning appeared for a moment;
a pregnant woman saw it and took it to be an evil spirit.
Terrified, she cried out loudly;
she fell to the ground and miscarried.
Consequently, the practice of eating only once a day was established.
Because they ate only one meal a day, the bhikṣus became emaciated and lacked strength.
Furthermore, it was permitted that after finishing a meal and before rising, they might eat fruits, vegetables, and other such items as supplements to assist their digestion;
subsequently, they would enter the city to beg for alms.
He obtained five types of auxiliary foods mixed with the primary meal;
he did not dare to eat them hastily.
He was emaciated from hunger and lacked strength.
Furthermore, he had heard that after finishing his meal, one must not receive the five kinds of formal food;
subsequently, he entered the city to beg for alms.
I obtained various vegetables mixed with the five kinds of food;
therefore, I did not dare to accept them immediately.
Consequently, I remained hungry and emaciated.
Furthermore, while they were eating and had not yet risen from their seats to perform the *pravāraṇā*,
they consumed five kinds of "resembling food" (*pratibimba-bhakṣya*) along with other vegetables mixed with the five types of "proper food" (*maulika-bhakṣya*).
Subsequently, the remains of the sick monk were left in a state of disarray.
Crows and birds vied with one another to come,
their clamor and cries filling the air.
Afterwards, listen as the attendant for the sick finishes eating and receives the *śeṣabhakta* (leftover food) rite.
If one eats this leftover food and is not a person who observes the one-meal-a-day precept,
one should receive it again from another bhikṣu who does observe the one-meal-a-day precept.
If the patient is one who eats but a single meal and has not yet eaten,
he may receive the *vighasa* (leftover food) according to the prescribed rite.
Furthermore, this is because the bhikṣu has various causes and conditions [for needing it].
Because of insufficient food, the practice of receiving the *khalupaścādbhaktika* (leftover-food) rule is permitted.
To receive this leftover-food rule, one should approach a bhikṣu who observes the single-meal practice (*ekāsanika*),
kneel on the right knee, and hold the food.
He should speak as follows:
"Venerable one, please remember:
I now request from you, Venerable One, the practice of receiving leftover food."
"Venerable sir, please leave me some leftovers;
once a monk who observes the one-meal practice has taken a single mouthful,
I shall then be able to eat."
If one receives the *khalupaścādbhakti* (leftover-food) procedure,
or if one receives the *khalupaścādbhakti* procedure in an improper manner, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one is already satiated, one may no longer receive the *khalupaścādbhakti* procedure.
Regarding the rule for receiving leftover food (*vighasa*):
if one has not yet finished eating and requests that the leftovers not be further accepted, one need not receive them again.
If one has not yet finished eating and does not request that they not be accepted, one may receive the leftover food.
If one places food from the bowl on the ground or upon the knees,
it does not constitute the practice of receiving leftover food;
to eat it in such a manner constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika).
Because one does not offer [the food] to a fellow bhikṣu who has already finished his single meal,
if the hands of two people do not reach each other, it is not called the "method of receiving leftover food" (vighasa-dharma),
as that bhikṣu who has finished his single meal would be unable to take it.
If one eats impure food, it is not called the practice of receiving leftover food (vighasa-kalpa).
Since neither [type of food] should be eaten,
those who eat either incur a *pāyattika* offense.
If one intends to eat the five types of side dishes while using the five types of staple foods,
and causes another to make them *vighasa* (leftover food), it does not constitute the ritual for receiving *vighasa*.
If one eats these five side dishes [in this manner], one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one intends to eat the five types of formal food or similar food,
yet uses the remaining two types of the fivefold food, it is likewise considered leftover.
In general, there are four modes of deportment.
Regarding the so-called postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down:
when a bhikṣu is traveling on a road, there is the rinsing of the mouth at the conclusion [of the journey] and at the time of eating.
When the meal is finished, one may receive the *vighasa* (leftover food) rule in its entirety.
If one is walking, one should receive it while walking;
one should not receive it while standing, sitting, or lying down.
To receive [food] but not eat it is called "receiving.
To eat it constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika).
This should also apply to standing, sitting, and lying down.
If you know that your skill is exhausted and you cannot form the characters, there is no need for further instruction.
Once you have finished eating, you should rest;
even if you have not yet risen, you must not eat again.
If one eats [in such a manner], one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense. Thirty-fifth:

if one knows that a bhikṣu has finished eating and, without the recipient having accepted the *vighasa-dharma*, one forcibly urges him to eat to his heart's content, it is a *pāyantika* offense because it causes distress to others. The rule regarding the *vighasa* (remnants) is concluded. There were two bhikṣus.
First, there is one who maintains the precepts; second, there is one who does not maintain them strictly.
As for the one who maintains the precepts, he sees that those who eat frequently are repeatedly censured and rebuked.
That person is unable to endure desire;
because it gives rise to faults, one knows not to accept leftover food,
lest it provoke irritation by being remembered while one is waiting.
If one strongly urges them to eat,
both parties commit a *pāyattika* offense at the time of eating; however,
there is no offense if one urges them while being unaware [of their refusal].
There are thirty-six instances for which eating in a separate group is permitted, provided there is a specific cause. These causes range from being ill to when a śramaṇa offers a meal.
At that time, Devadatta, intending to destroy the Saṃgha, practiced the five supernormal powers and various transformations.
The sovereign of the land turned his heart toward him;
the entire realm submitted to him,
and offerings were made in full abundance.
He gave food and clothing to the bhikṣus;
those of recent training and shallow understanding took what was beneficial for them and departed.
For this reason, one does not permit eating in a separate assembly;
it is to destroy the power of a wicked assembly and to prevent the schism of the Saṃgha.
It is for the sake of enabling laypeople to obtain great merit from the field of blessings that is the Saṃgha;
and for the sake of ensuring that the assembly remains harmonious and joyful with minds free from duality.
There are, in total, three kinds of realms.
Regarding the boundary of the *karmavācanā*, the village boundary, and the open space boundary:
if a bhikṣu or a layperson is within the boundary of the *karmavācanā*,
whether in a monastery or in a layperson’s house.
If four persons are invited separately and eat together in one place while staying in different rooms,
this is called eating in a separate group.
One who eats [in such a manner] commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one person among the pure assembly gives even a small portion to the group,
or if it is given to the Saṃgha, there must be one donor for each individual.
If one makes a general offering to the monks within the boundary,
yet gives food separately at various locations,
those who eat it are entirely without offense.
If, within the boundaries of a village,
two donors each provide a meal for the community at a separate location,
with four members of the community at each site.
It is also called "eating separately from the assembly.
If one eats such food, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
This refers to two separate groups of monks receiving offerings of rice and other food as distinct meals within the boundaries of a village.
If one eats, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
it does not constitute the offense of eating separately from the community (*pṛthaggaṇabhojana*).
This applies when invitations are mutually exchanged between two locations.
Among the assembly, one person was without offense.
Furthermore, when the two assemblies within the upper two realms were eating,
three people from each finished their meal.
If one person eats later,
there is no offense.
If within the boundary, four teachers and disciples share both property and food.
This is not an illegal act and is not termed "eating separately from the community.
There is no offense for a sick person eating separately from the community.
If one is occupied with making robes, it may hinder the practice of begging for food.
Because begging for alms interferes with the making of robes,
there is no offense in eating separately from the community when making robes;
however, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense if the three robes are insufficient.
Furthermore, it is permitted for one to carry [the bowl] while walking because walking causes extreme fatigue,
or because one might fear missing the proper time.
Alternatively, it may be because a suitable companion is difficult to find;
or out of fear of losing their companion and the setting of the sun,
they come from twenty *li* away to listen.
Within the village boundary, eating separately from the community is not an offense;
this clarifies that one may obtain food by going [to eat].
However, having come yesterday, one may not do so today as well.
If there is fear of various dangers regarding a journey by boat,
or if one is exhausted, eating separately from the group is not an offense.
This also applies during times when the great assembly gathers.
That is to say, from a maximum of ten million down to eight people,
they are permitted to listen to the Dharma due to the causal conditions for hearing the teaching.
At one time, when the world was not prosperous and the multitude of people was vast and dense,
one should speak these words: "In these times of scarcity,
though the multitude is dense, food and drink are difficult to obtain."
For example, there is no offense for one who begs for food separately from the group.
Furthermore, regarding the resident and guest monks:
if there are four resident monks and three guest monks.
Regarding the "old" who receive food from a separate assembly:
because the "old" constitute the fundamental Saṃgha,
there are four "guests" and three "old" members.
A guest must not eat apart from the community.
One may invite a single senior monk;
a śramaṇa is one who has gone forth from among the non-Buddhist paths.
The renunciant brahmin was the nephew of King Bimbisāra.
Because the king was a follower of the Buddha, he wished to invite bhikṣus;
however, because the bhikṣus had established the precepts, they did not dare to accept the invitation arbitrarily.
The Buddha, in order to shatter the arrogance of the non-Buddhists,
permitted [the monks] to accept invitations without committing an offense;
although they were to eat separately from the assembly, the invitations were extended to them personally.
One does not eat by oneself.

If one does not personally request [food] but serves it oneself,
there is a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of receiving the invitation;
there is no offense at the time of eating.
If one does not personally request [food] nor personally serve it,
one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of receiving the invitation,
and commits a *pāyattika* offense at the time of eating.

Nanda’s disciple was named Dharma.

meaning they perform all *karmavācanā* (formal acts), recite the *Prātimokṣa*, and perform the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) together.
If one stays overnight within the same four types of dwellings as fourteen kinds of persons involved in all monastic affairs—
whether it be those who teach the Dharma or those from whom one receives the Dharma— one commits a *pāyattika* offense for each instance.
If one provides robes, alms bowls, food, bedding, or medicinal requisites,
or if one receives them from such a person, one falls [into an offense] for each instance.
In all cases of sharing livestock or engaging in joint activities, one falls [into an offense] for each individual item.
If, while staying overnight together, one lies down and then gets up, or gets up and then lies down again,
one commits a *pāyattika* offense for every instance of lying down and getting up.
If one does not lie down at all throughout the night, one commits a *dukkaṭa* offense.
57. The novice monk Upananda, named Māka, committed a grave act of sexual misconduct.
Having done so, he gave rise to a wicked and false view, saying:
"Sexual desire cannot obstruct the path."
Having assembled the community, and because he did not abandon his evil and heterodox views,
they performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to carry out his *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment),
sending him away.
This cessation is not seen.
The group of six bhikṣus, knowing this, continued to keep it;
this will lead to the growth of heterodoxy and the harboring of evil, which cannot be restrained.
Therefore, it is not permitted to keep [such a person], nor to converse with them, work together with them, or share a dwelling and sleep with them.
The meaning of "conversing, working together, sharing a dwelling, and sleeping" is the same as explained above.
For each of these acts, the offense is a *pāyattika* (falling away), as described above.
If a *parivāsika* śrāmaṇera regains right view,
his confession shall be accepted.
If a *parivāsika* śrāmaṇera earnestly reforms and repents of himself, [he shall likewise be pardoned].
One should request to dwell in dependence upon the community.
If, out of sincerity and out of compassion for the community, they grant permission to dwell in dependence upon the community,
it shall be according to the rules for laypeople.
They shall never receive the precepts for the rest of their lives;
they may share in the communal food, but shall not receive a portion of the robes.
The donor may give it to him and he may accept it;
the teacher must not take the voting tally (*śalākā*).

(58) If one takes, or causes another to take, a jewel, a counterfeit jewel, or what is called a jewel—unless it is within a monastic cell (*vihāra*) or within a residence (*āvāsa*)—one falls [into an offense]. There was a certain poor man.
He encountered a hidden treasure and suddenly became immensely wealthy;
the king then sought to execute him and seize it.
Recalling the Buddha’s words,
he was spared from death;
now, because of his reproach regarding the taking of jewels, he has been granted this [opportunity].
The precepts had not yet been formulated;
later, when the young boys saw Baddhananda,
they recognized his greedy attachment.
Desiring to admonish him together with others,
he scattered jewels upon the road and remained hidden to observe him in secret.
Nanda took it immediately,
concealed it, and departed.
The boys seized him together and brought him to be handed over to the official on watch.
The investigating official believed in the Buddha;
he rebuked [the criminals] and released them.
Consequently, malicious rumors spread in great confusion.
Thereafter, the precepts were established.
Regarding the thirty matters concerning personal possession,
it is now ordained that kings and others may possess all types of authentic jewels.
Those that resemble jewels are copper, iron, white tin, lead, and pewter;
counterfeit pearls are also made of leather or glue.
You, however, are taking all genuine jewels for yourselves.
If one instructs another to take hold of them, one commits an offense of falling (pāyattika) in all such cases.
Regarding ornaments for men or women, or weapons and implements made from imitation jewels:
if one takes hold of them oneself or instructs another to take hold of them, one likewise commits an offense of falling in all such cases.
There is no offense in taking hold of ornaments, vessels, or weapons. You,
Mṛgāramātṛ, having entered the monastery to visit the Buddha,
removed your precious robes and entrusted them to your attendant.
A servant who was skilled in the methods of medicine forgot his robes and departed.
The Buddha commanded Ānanda to have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) look after and store them.
Because of this, he further permitted that one should take what is appropriate when there is a valid reason.
Whatever is within the boundary of the Saṃgha should be measured and stored by a *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things allowable);
if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, one should measure and store it oneself.
One may accept [the gift] in order to avoid censure and to protect the Buddha-dharma.
At the time of taking it, one should think:
"When the owner asks for it, I shall return it."
When the owner comes to claim it, one should examine him and ask:
"How much was your property? What were its characteristics?
If the characteristics match, then it should be returned.
If it is not the case that the signs [of suitability] are absent, one should entrust the matter to a virtuous bhikṣu for execution.
If someone comes to demand it, one should inquire about the signs and return it to them.
If no one comes to claim it for five or six years,
it should be entered into the property of the Sangha of the four directions.
If the original owner later comes to claim it, [it should be returned].
One shall restore items belonging to the Sangha of the four quarters.
Regarding items found within a monastery, this refers to monks;
if such items are found in the house of a layperson, one should take them and return them as described above.
Five or six years later, he used that very spot to provide bedding for the community of monks.
When the owner later came to reclaim it,
[the monks] returned the property to him.
The questions regarding the examination of the requisites are all as before.
To take up ornaments or precious objects belonging to the Three Jewels to fashion them into scriptures or images constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one takes them with the intention of making such things, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one sees a lost treasure in the two aforementioned locations, one must not take hold of it oneself;
to take hold of it oneself constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. One may have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) take hold of it, in which case there is no offense.
Whenever one holds bows, swords, sharp weapons, or any instruments used for harming living beings,
one must confess these before the assembly.
To hold shields, armor, or other military equipment for the purpose of protecting oneself constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Fifty-nine: When obtaining new robes, one should apply three kinds of dyeing to ruin their original color.
Baddhālaka wore his robes and quarreled with a child over a profit, causing the child to feel resentment and exclusion.
Because of this, he rebuked them,
yet had not yet laid down a precept.
Later, some bhikṣus traveled together with merchants.
They were all plundered and wounded together;
their clothes were stripped away.
The thieves, having faith in the Buddha-dharma, wished to return the robes to the bhikṣus, but they could not distinguish which belonged to whom.
He returned naked and reported this to the Buddha,
who then established the precept:
if one obtains new cloth, it must be discolored in three ways.
Because it differs from the [other] brahmins,
and because it has departed from the fondness for greed;
if one obtains another's old garment, it is called a "new garment" at the moment of first acquisition.
One should apply one of three types of dyed colors—
either blue, mud-colored, or rust-colored—
and according to whichever is obtained, it should be purified in two ways.
If one obtains a pure *kaṣāya* robe, it is purified by means of *nīla*;
if one obtains a pure *nīla* robe, it is purified by means of *mañjiṣṭha*;
if one obtains a pure *mañjiṣṭha* robe, it is purified by means of both *nīla* and *kaṣāya*.
If one obtains yellow robes that are purified by being dyed with indigo,
the same applies to obtaining red or white robes.
This is true for all bhikṣu’s clothing, bedding, and sitting mats.
All things should be purified in this manner;
to use what is unpurified constitutes a *pāyattika* offense,
and to try it on for a moment constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one obtains a pure robe and patches it with impure material,
if one inserts even a single stitch, it becomes purified;
if one simply patches it in various places, each such spot becomes purified.
If one obtains dyed robes of two kinds of discolored hues,
they are purified by tearing and pulling;
tearing makes them firm and stable.
Because he is distinct from other brahmins,
he may enter the village wearing the great robe (saṃghāṭī),
but he may not enter wearing two robes.
One who enters [the boundary] commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Within the boundary, one must not prostrate to the Buddha while wearing the *saṃghāṭī*; to do so constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The *saṃghāṭī* must necessarily be made by cutting the cloth into pieces, sewing them together, and hemming the edges.
If one does not cut [the cloth] into patches, one may not accept or maintain it.
There is no offense for sewing two uncut robes together.
If one is poor and lacks a great robe (saṃghāṭī), [this applies].
One may possess five *niṣīdana* robes.
If they are stitched together, one should maintain them; if they are not stitched together, one should purify them by relinquishing them.
When one’s life is about to end, one should have someone remove them and return them to the community of robes.
Among the three robes, one should give the middle-sized one to the attendant who cares for the sick;
even if [the sick monk] does not maintain formal possession of it, one should take that middle-sized one and give it to the attendant.

Regarding the offense of falling into transgression (pācittiya) for failing to provide food during the sixty-day period preceding the half-month: King Bimbisāra had three channels of water, of which he shared the upper channel with the community of monks.
Monks frequently bathed, thereby neglecting their duties for the King;
therefore, the precept was established,
limiting [bathing] to once every half-month.
After the limit [of the cold season], one will fall ill if one does not bathe during the heat;
when the heat begins,
one may bathe as one pleases.
One month and a half remaining of spring,
one month of early summer,
and furthermore, the impurity during the time of illness.
When the wind blows, it stirs up dust;
when it rains, it wets one's clothes;
and through walking about, one becomes soiled and defiled.
There is no offense in listening while bathing.
When bathing, one should wear one's robes,
kneel with the right knee on the ground, and join the palms together.
He addressed a certain bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind:
I have such-and-such a reason for needing to bathe."
If the teacher is present, one should inform the teacher;
if there is no teacher, one should inform the senior monk;
if there is no senior monk, one should speak to the junior monk.
However, one should not kneel with the knees apart.
All that ought to be done is to be performed in this manner.
If one has fifty years of seniority (pañcāśad-varṣa), when crossing the boundary or during major affairs, one should announce it and speak accordingly.
Minor matters need not be reported.
Therefore it is said: "Sixty-first:
Taking the life of an animal—above, by sprinkling water containing insects upon grass or soil."
First, one uses water containing insects for oneself;
though truly lacking compassion,
the intention is not to cause harm.
This refers to Kāḷodāyin’s taking the life of a bird out of arrogance and a desire to display his skill;
whether acting oneself, instructing another, or sending an agent—
these are the three modes of killing.
When that life is severed, the bhikṣu commits a pāyattika offense.
Furthermore, there are three ways of killing: either by means of the body or by means other than the body.
By these three matters, one harms sentient beings;
if they die, one commits a *pāyattika* offense;
if they do not die, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Even down to the very first moment of conception,
when one employs the means of killing through the causal conditions of bodily, verbal, or mental karma, if the person dies,
one commits an offense of falling (pāyattika).
The offense of *dukkaṭa* for not dying [from the transgression].

Because of sixty-two [instances], one causes another bhikṣu to repent, even to a slight degree; by causing distress, one commits the offense of *pāyattika*. The group of six and the group of seventeen quarreled with discordant minds.
He constantly spoke with contempt and jealousy, saying:
"You have not yet reached twenty years of age to receive full ordination;
you have not attained the precepts and are no śramaṇa."
By means of this, one causes him distress,
leading him to doubt and regret.
In general, to distress a great bhikṣu by means of these six matters constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika).
First, the lifetime;
second, receiving the precepts;
third, transgression.
The four questions,
the five objects,
and the six dharmas.
He said to another:
"When did you grow pubic hair?
And when did it emerge?"
At what time did you receive the precepts?
Who served as your three masters? Did you receive the precepts within a group of five or a group of ten?
In what location did you receive the precepts?
"Is it within the boundary or outside the boundary?
He answered truthfully,
whereupon [the other] provoked him, saying:
"You were born during the reign of King So-and-so;
at that time, hair grew [upon your body],
and at that time, you received the precepts."
A certain person acted as the three preceptors;
those who received the precepts within that boundary did not obtain them and were not śramaṇas.
That person then gave rise to doubt and regret.
If one does not give rise to each and every offense, one falls into transgression.
Furthermore, it is said:
"If you violate the precepts of the latter four categories, you are no longer a śramaṇa."
Furthermore, each instance constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika).
He was also asked where he resided,
and he answered truthfully.
He then said,
"Go to such-and-such a woman or such-and-such a nun; your sitting,
rising, and speech are not those of a śramaṇa."
Furthermore, you and such-and-such a bhikṣu using various kinds of requisites for personal needs are not śramaṇas.
Moreover, during the period of the *kaṭhina* robe, you repeatedly eat and keep extra robes; these are not the ways of a śramaṇa.
If he causes doubt or regret,
he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya) for each individual statement.
Outside of these six matters, if he uses other matters to cause a bhikkhu or another person to feel doubt or regret, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

63. To strike with the hand in pain constitutes a *pācittiya* offense. There was once a young child among the group of seventeen who, unable to endure his itching, struck it repeatedly with his fingers.
Consequently, his breath ceased and he died;
both [the perpetrator and the victim] incur a *pāyattika* offense for that death.
If it is a single finger, it is a single *pāyattika*.
There are ten fingers and ten instances of falling [into offense].
If one points with a finger or extends a finger, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (突吉羅).
If one strikes or rubs [the body] with wood, stone, or other objects that are not parts of one's own body, one commits a *duṣkṛta*.
If it is painful but not itchy, and one does not cause the other to faint, there is no offense.
Regarding the sixty-fourth rule, "playing in water," there is an offense of *pāyattika*: the group of seventeen monks entered the water intending to play.
King Prasenajit saw this and laughed,
saying to Queen Mallikā,
"Look at whom you revere."
The lady addressed the Buddha.
Thereupon, the Buddha established a precept:
"If one plays in the water, there are eight difficulties."
First, one produces joy for oneself;
second, one produces pleasure for oneself;
third, one laughs.
Fourth, playing games;
fifth, splashing water;
sixth, causing others to experience pleasure.
Eighth, causing others to laugh:
each instance constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
This includes even drawing with a finger on water on a bed or on a tray.
Each instance constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one wishes to learn how to swim across a difficult passage,
there is no offense if one crosses directly.
65. To stay overnight in the same dwelling as a woman constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
While Ānanda was traveling, he stayed at a courtesan’s house as evening approached.
There are four types of dwellings.
First, universal covering and obstructing;
second, universal obstructing but non-universal covering;
third, non-universal covering and obstructing.
Regarding the four types of partially covered dwellings:
among these four kinds of houses, if one sleeps together with a woman, a non-human female, or a female animal, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one rises and then lies down again, one commits a *pāyattika* offense for each instance.
If both are asleep, it is suffering.
If one is asleep, it is called "having spent the night" (*sāyāhna*),
because not having passed the night constitutes "having spent the night."
If both [the monk and the woman] remain awake throughout the night, there is no offense.
If there is a woman staying overnight in another's house and there is a hole in the wall large enough for a kitten to enter, it is an offense of falling (pāyattika).
If elephants are either reclining or standing, it is called "resting.
If camels, oxen, sheep, or goats are either lying down or standing, it is called "resting.
It is likewise when they all sleep together in one sleep, or none of them sleep at all.

66. Causing another bhikṣu to be terrified, or causing someone else to cause him to be terrified, even up to doing so in jest, constitutes a pāyattika offense. Regarding the attendants of the Tathāgata, there have been seven in total throughout his life.
Ānanda was at the very rear.
There was an attendant named Hastidāsa.
During the first watch of the night, he waited for the Buddha;
as long as the Buddha had not yet returned to his room,
he did not enter first.
He was then immediately seized and confined, causing him to experience the terror of becoming a ghost.
Because of this, the Buddha established a precept:
one must not frighten others.
There are six things that cause fear in others:
the various objects of dread,
namely form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
That is to say, through various arts and crafts, one produces diverse objects with [specific] colors, sounds, and scents;
these are not always fragrant.
Or it is said:
"What do you eat now?
If you eat such mixed food, you will surely contract a malignant disease;
or else you must discipline your body to make it firm, supple, smooth, and slippery."
They touch others to cause them alarm and fear, or say:
"You have violated numerous rules of the Dharma."
One will inevitably enter the three miserable realms.
By means of these six matters, one intimidates other bhikṣus;
whether they are intimidated or not, it constitutes one offense of falling (pāyattika).
Excluding these six matters,
if a teacher commits [an offense] against another through other matters,
he incurs a *duṣkṛta*. Furthermore, if one causes fear in others— whether humans, non-humans, or animals— through other matters, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
67. Hiding Various Articles of Daily Use, Even Down to Laughter and Play.
There was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha;
the group of six bhikṣus hid the robes and bowls of the group of seventeen bhikṣus so that they could not join the assembly.
On account of this, the precept was established:
"In general, to conceal the belongings of another bhikṣu,
whether doing it oneself or instructing another to do so."
Whether out of malice or in jest, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
To hide another's robe, bowl, door-latch, leather sandals, or needle-case such that they cannot be immediately recovered constitutes a *dukkaṭa*;
however, if it is a hollow needle-case containing thread, and it is found upon searching, there is no offense.
To do so entirely constitutes a *duṣkṛta*. 68.
To take back robes that one has given to the five groups of renunciants constitutes a *pāyattika*. The group of six was indolent;
they did not make their own robes.
He gave the robe to the group of five,
without specifying whether it was a gift or not;
the other, having received it, then deceitfully completed the act of making it his own.
Once it was completed, he seized it and caused him distress and anger; because of this,
the precept was established.
If one gives robes to the fivefold assembly and they do not return them,
yet one seizes them, one commits an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*),
because it causes obstruction and disorder for others.
Because of disputes,
the five methods for purifying gifts (pañca pariśuddhi-dāna) that were previously permitted were later superseded by the prohibition against purifying gifts of extra robes (atireka-cīvara).

After an extra robe had been formally dedicated through the ritual of *śuddhaka-dāna*, it was taken by another who had not yet attained the stage of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), which gave rise to a dispute.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be given in the presence [of the recipient]."
Nor should one give it to two or three people,
for their minds would be distracted and unsettled.
One should carefully consider and give it only to a person of good character.
Whether it is present before one or not, one may relinquish it at will according to the procedure for relinquishing an article involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika),
or it may also be rendered pure (viśuddha).
If a bhikṣu who has formally accepted an extra robe (atirekacīvara) gives it to one of the group of six (ṣaḍvargika),
and that person, having received it, does not return it,
the Buddha said:
One should confiscate the instruction and perform a *pratideśanīya* (confession of an offense).
Because of this, it is permitted that robes used regularly may be made subject to the *svayam-vaśa-pariśuddhi* (purification by one's own will).
Whether they are given to another or kept for oneself, they should not be returned.
Giving it away is treated like the forfeiture of an object.
(69) To slander another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense involving forfeiture. Previously, Cīrṇabhūmi falsely accused Dābhya with the four *pārājika* offenses.
The second slander was not established.
Now, this slander has occurred;
because of this, the precept is formulated.
In general, regarding those who slander a pure bhikṣu with groundless and depraved teachings,
there are eleven types of offenses and five types of non-offenses.
As for the eleven types of offenses:
If one has not seen, heard, or doubted;
or if one has seen but forgotten, heard but forgotten, or doubted but forgotten;
or if one has heard and believes it.
If one hears [the teaching] but does not believe it;
or having heard it, claims to have seen it;
or having doubted it, claims to have heard it.
These are called the eleven kinds of offenses.
Regarding the five kinds of non-offenses:
if one has seen, heard, or suspected this matter [to be otherwise].
Having seen, one does not forget;
having heard, one does not forget.
These are called the five kinds of non-transgression.
It is the same for an impure bhikṣu accusing a pure bhikṣu.
There are ten types of offenses for groundlessly slandering a pure bhikṣu;
these exclude the cases of seeing or forgetting, as described above.
There are four cases where there is no offense.
With the exception of seeing or forgetting, the rest is as stated above.
This applies likewise to a pure bhikṣu who appears to be impure.

"Traveling by the same path with a woman, even as far as a single village": while the previous rule prohibited traveling with a *bhikṣuṇī*, this rule prohibits [traveling with] a laywoman (*avadātavasana*).
[This concerns] the bhikṣu Kālodāyin.
As he was traveling toward Vaiśālī,
he went along the same road as a woman who had been sent away by her husband.
Later, the husband searched for her and saw them together on the path.
Suspicion and resentment led to an assault;
because of this, the precept was established:
if one makes an appointment with a woman to travel together by water or land.
Traveling from village to village constitutes an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
Turning back midway also constitutes an offense of downfall.
Traveling ten *li* through an open space constitutes an offense of downfall.
If one returns by the central route, it is sudden; if not,
and if there are men traveling at a great distance from one another.
If one travels with the king’s consort as a companion, there is no offense.
Seventy-one: traveling along a road with a bandit acquaintance as far as a village. Formerly, some bhikṣus lost their way while traveling through the wilderness.
He encountered a wicked bandit who sought to have him as a companion.
He seized the bandit and delivered him to the authorities;
after the matter was settled, he was released.
If one makes an appointment with a thief to travel together by water or land,
from village to village, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense;
if one turns back midway, it is a *thullaccaya*.
If one travels ten *li* through an open space and commits an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*), it is a violation;
if one turns back midway, it is not [an offense] unless there was a prior intention.
If one is sent across a dangerous place by bandits, there is no offense.

If a person less than seventy-two years old who has not yet reached twenty receives full ordination, that person does not obtain the precepts; such monks are to be censured. The group of seventeen bhikṣus were under twenty.
Maudgalyāyana had conferred the full precepts upon him while he was still very young;
moreover, being the son of a wealthy and pleasure-seeking family,
he cried out like a small child when overcome by hunger at the hour of *pradoṣa*.
Therefore, it is not permitted for one who has not yet reached twenty years of age to receive the precepts,
because they have not yet attained maturity and are unable to endure hardship.
When receiving the precepts within the Saṃgha, one asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?
If not yet full [twenty], he should answer: "I am not."
If one confers the precepts upon such a person, they do not obtain the precepts;
the preceptor and the assembly of monks incur offenses,
and those who associate with or dwell together with them also incur offenses.
If one causes a schism in the Saṃgha for the sake of joining with others, one commits the offense of *steya* (theft).
If it is done with another intention, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If [the conditions] are not yet fulfilled, one says "no."
If [the assembly] is complete, this person obtains the precepts,
while the preceptor and the Sangha incur an offense.
There is no offense if one performs tasks and dwells together [with them].
If asked whether it is complete, one should answer "it is not complete."
This person obtains the precepts; however,
the preceptor and the monastic community incur an offense,
as do those who share duties and dwell together with them.
If he answers "Yes" when asked "Is it full?",
this person obtains the precepts.
The preceptor incurs no offense;
those who live and work together with him also incur no offense.
This is because one who is less than seven years [junior] or over sixty years [of age] is incapable of enduring hardships.
If one disparages or harms the Buddha-dharma, they shall not be ordained;
even if ordained, they shall not receive the precepts.
Both the one who ordains and the one who receives the precepts commit the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
73. Digging the ground with one's own hands causes [a being] to fall [into hell]. A bhikṣu named Abhīra dug the ground.
Because an outsider with false views remarked that the earth possesses life, [the Buddha] established this rule out of reproach.
One must not accept heterodox teachings.
This has already been explained in detail above by the Triple World Dharma Protector.
There are two kinds of stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding "growing" and "not growing":
in countries with much rain, plants grow in the eighth month;
that is to say, there are four months each for spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
"Birth" refers to the end of spring and the beginning of summer;
each consists of two months.
To exclude these is called "non-birth."
Furthermore, in collapsed mounds, anthills, or where the soil at the base of stones is moist, grass does not grow; this condition is designated as "unborn.
Conversely, that which is different from this is designated as "born.
Whether one digs it oneself or instructs another to dig it, [it is born].
Each individual offense constitutes a *pāyattika*;
each instance of drawing on the ground constitutes a *dukkaṭa*,
even down to the size of a mustard seed.
Each instance constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, if a bhikṣu acts as a master craftsman for the purpose of constructing a Buddhist stūpa or a monastic dwelling,

74. Accepting an invitation for the *pravāraṇā* for four months, up to and including the exception of an individual *pravāraṇā*: Śrīmān invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

one may take whatever is needed according to one's requirements,
with full liberty in all matters.
The group of six bhikṣus, though not ill, exceeded the limit and sought further;
they sought ghee, oil, honey, fine delicacies, and superior medicines.
When these superior medicines were exhausted, they did not comply with their needs and desires.
They further gave rise to anger and verbal abuse,
leading to outward resentment;
for this reason, the precept was established.
Once the limit has passed, one may no longer seek [medicines].
If a donor regularly invites [the Sangha]— such as when a father dies and his son succeeds him— to allow the monks to take medicines at will,
this is called "constant self-indulgence" (nitya-pravāraṇā).
If medicine for the summer four-month retreat is originally offered to the Saṃgha,
and one seeks to prepare it during the first month,
then the summer retreat shall be observed for three months.
The first month and two days of the winter supplement have been determined;
the three months of the winter supplement are completed.
Of the four months of summer, none have yet been determined.
In winter they receive another four months;
in summer they seek [animals] by hunting in winter so that the four-month period may be fulfilled.
This is called the frequent *pravāraṇā*.
It is the same for the four months of winter and spring.
For the remaining months, receiving [the robes] month by month is also a frequent *pravāraṇā*.
One should request [the *pravāraṇā*] from those who are not part of the assembly; this is called the "individual *pravāraṇā*.
Once the three requests have been made, the four-month period of invitation is concluded.
If one who is free from illness further seeks out four kinds of superior medicines— such as those that are nourishing, digestive, or otherwise desirable—
and obtains them, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; it does not constitute a *dukkaṭa*.
If one requests bitter medicines such as harītakī for the purpose of purging,
whether or not they are obtained constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; however, this does not apply if the request is made due to illness.
If one seeks it from a relative or if the person gives it of their own accord,

Seventy-fifth: When the time for reciting the precepts has come, if one says, "I have not yet studied these precepts; first I must ask those who recite the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā," one falls [into an offense]. The monastic precepts for monks and nuns have both similarities and differences.
If the bhikṣuṇī precepts differ, they are established by convening the two assemblies;
if the precepts are the same, they are established by convening the saṃgha.
Subsequently, one should inform them of the decision.
The Elder Vajra, pure and virtuous, was appointed by the Saṃgha to go to the bhikṣuṇīs and proclaim the common precepts:
"Excellent, O bhikṣuṇīs!"
They all accepted and upheld [the teachings].
However, Thullanandā, treating the instruction lightly, refused it, saying:
"I shall consult the three types of Dharma masters."
Because they assembled the community and likewise established the precepts together,
when the precepts were recited, it was declared that both monks and nuns would fall [into offense] equally.
If, when hearing the exposition of the five classes of offenses or other rules of the Vinaya-mātṛkā,
one speaks as follows:
Each [of these] constitutes a downfall.
Furthermore, when other sūtras are being recited, one does not receive them into one's mind, thinking:
"I shall first question those who have memorized the three kinds of sūtras."
In each and every case of a *dukkaṭa* offense,
the three types of sūtras may either explain the precepts (*śīla*) or explain the Dharma (*dharma*).
When this sutra was being preached, some heard the precepts but did not accept them,
each falling into transgression;
others heard the Dharma but did not accept it, committing a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The *Mātṛkā-vibhaṅga* analyzes the characteristics of dharmas as does the *Abhidharma*.
For twelve years, the precepts for the seven classes of followers had not yet been codified,
nor were there established the rules regarding offenses that obstruct the Path.
After twelve years, all were bound by the same precepts;
alternatively, they might be bound by different precepts, such as when the four types [of ordination] were established, the seven assemblies were bound together.
Thereafter, only the oral instructions were proclaimed, and no further separate categories of rules were formulated.
Although they differ in that they obstruct the Path,
they are the same in this regard: if a bhikṣu wishes to hear the benefits of the Dharma,
he should train in these precepts and should also inquire about them.
When people recite these three kinds of sūtras, they should not harbor thoughts of contempt toward one another;
it is only that they do not receive the precepts.

When the seventy-six bhikṣus heard the chaotic dispute, they stood listening in silence, thinking: "I shall remember and retain what these bhikṣus say, lest I fall into an offense. After the group of seventeen and the group of six had finished their quarrel, [the others remained silent].
The group of seventeen monks spoke together in a secluded place,
saying to one another,
"The group of six monks is arrogant and ill-reputed."
"If we act with one mind, they will find no opportunity against us.
When the group of six thieves heard this,
they raised their voices and their countenances changed.
He rebuked the group of seventeen bhikṣus and, on that account, established the rule:
"One must not listen to the speech of others in silence;
if one hears it, one falls [into an offense]."
Do not listen eavesdroppingly;
whether it be good or evil, one must never steal to hear.
Those who steal to hear shall all fall [into ruin].
To prevent disputes:
if one is in harmony, or if one encounters or hears [the teaching] while practicing, there is no offense.
Seventy-seventh: when the Saṃgha is settling a matter, to rise and leave in silence constitutes a *pācittiya*. Sevanti was greedy and accumulated many faults.
The assembly wished to punish the offense.
Five men went out on patrol;
one man accompanied them as an assistant from behind.
When the assembly was chanting together,
the assistant departed secretly,
so that the group remained entirely unaware.
The *karmavācanā* was then completed.
After the *karmavācanā*, the person assisting [the candidate] declared it invalid;
because of this, the precept was established.
It is said that for all *karmas*, one must perform the *pravāraṇā*.
