he who departs in silence commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If one has urgent business such as defecation or urination,
or if one entrusts the matter to another person,
there is no offense provided that one does not depart from the hearing or receiving [of the instruction].
To obstruct legal proceedings by aiding evil and hindering the good constitutes an offense of *duṣkṛta* (突) in all cases.
Whenever there is a formal assembly or a gathering of the community, one must not depart in silence;
to do so also constitutes an offense.
Seventy-eighth: Causing another bhikṣu to fall [into an offense] by being disrespectful.
While the Venerable Elder was preaching the sūtras and the Dharma, Chanda was irreverent and lacked a sense of awe;
he did not wait for the discourse to conclude, but interrupted with irrelevant speech.
On account of this, the precept was established;
a formal motion followed by three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) was performed,
and that bhikṣu was recorded as one who does not comply with respectful service.
Whenever one listens to the preaching of the Dharma or the instruction on the five categories of precepts,
speaking in a distracted manner and showing disrespect constitutes two types of offenses against the Saṃgha;
these matters of disrespect have not yet been formally recorded.
Furthermore, he did not instruct [the offender] regarding the *dukkaṭa* offense.
Having already declared that disrespect constitutes a *pāyattika* offense,
[he now addresses] the case where a senior monk shows disrespect toward a junior monk.
Whether [the offense] has already been formally declared or not yet declared, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (transgression).
79. Drinking Alcohol: The Ṣaḍabhijña Arhat Śāgara subdued an evil dragon;
his fame was already renowned throughout various kingdoms, and they vied with one another to offer him excellent food.
There was a woman who,
fearing that [the food] would not digest,
gave Śāgata wine mixed with water and honey.
Having drunk, he fell into a drunken sleep;
his corpse lay in the middle of the road,
while his robes, bowl, and six personal effects were scattered across the ground like stars.
The Buddha encountered this while traveling and consequently established the precept;
for because of alcohol, one breaks all precepts and commits all manner of evil.
Furthermore, although one who has committed the four pārājika offenses cannot split the Saṃgha, it is because people do not believe him.
Seeing that all seven classes of followers collectively bind themselves to this fixed precept,
one must not drink even a small blade of grass or a single drop of water [if it is impure].
There are two kinds of liquor:
wood liquor and grain liquor.
Grain liquor is made from rice, yeast, and various blended medicinal herbs.
There are wines made solely from the roots, stalks, flowers, and leaves of trees,
unmixed with rice or yeast,
yet possessing the color, flavor, and fragrance of wine.
If one drinks anything that can intoxicate people, one falls into an offense for every swallow;
whether drinking or tasting it, one commits a *pāyattika* offense with each gulp.
If one eats dregs or yeast that can intoxicate people, one commits a *pāyattika* offense for all of them.
Every swallow constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Among the eighty [rules], entering a village to receive alms without informing the other bhikṣus constitutes a *pāyattika*, except for a great cause. Before midday, one should go begging for food.
Neither the clergy nor the laity found this strange.
Later in the day, he emerged again;
his interference with their practice led to public censure.
The non-Buddhists were indignant and disparaged him.
After the Buddha had already rebuked them,
Kālodāyin later entered the village after the midday meal.
Driven by darkness, he harmed others and buried their corpses in a mound of excrement;
when his deeds were exposed,
those who suffered the consequences were numerous, as he had acted in silence at an improper time.
Such are its faults.
Whenever a monk goes to reside, he must rely on a village to establish a *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary).
Within the *mahā-sīmā* established in reliance upon a village, there are three locations.
The fundamental location:
that which is near a village is called a "village.
It refers to a monastic dwelling where those who delight in meditation find purity.
A secluded and remote, empty, and quiet place is called an *āraṇyaka* location.
A dwelling where a monk who manages the storehouse and affairs resides is called a *vihāra*.
If a bhikṣu proceeds from one place to enter a village without having announced his intention,
he commits an offense of expiation (pāyattika) for each individual house; for every alley, large or small, that he passes through,
he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one departs from the monastery to enter a village,
and having entered the village, returns to the monastery;
or if one goes to a place for meditative practice or to an official government office.
If one enters a village immediately after having previously announced one's intention, one falls into an offense.
For every single large or small alleyway one passes through upon entering, there is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for each.
It is the same if one proceeds from a place of meditation toward a village for official business.
Within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), among the three locations, he formally announces his entry into the village and his return to the three locations.
He then re-enters using that same prior announcement,
thereby increasing the benefit of his coming and going.
If it is wholesome and not reported, there is no offense.
This is also the case when going to another monastic residence.
Later, a bhikṣu deposited his robe in another's house.
A house of his caught fire.
A bhikṣu went to retrieve [an item],
and on the way, he thought to himself:
He arrived without having announced his presence.
Upon returning, he informed the Saṃgha that the [structure] had already been completely consumed by fire.
For this reason, it is further permitted not to announce one's departure when there is an urgent cause.
If a fire breaks out in a village,
or if any one of the eight calamities occurs, it is not an offense to depart silently.
If one has an illness, or if one must visit another who is ill,
or if there are matters concerning the Three Jewels or other such conditions that require action at an inappropriate time,
one may go after having informed [the preceptor]. All such cases are permitted.
If there is no bhikṣu present, one may speak to the other six groups [of practitioners].
With the exception of paying homage to the Triple Gem and the procedures for the major and minor necessities such as using tooth-sticks,
everything else should be reported to one's teacher.
If there is no teacher, one should inform the senior monk;
if there is no senior monk, one should speak to the junior monk.
To fail to inform anyone constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one is fifty years of age, one must announce when leaving the boundary or undertaking major matters;
for minor matters, there is no need to announce them.
Regarding the offense of visiting other households before or after a meal when invited by eighty-one bhikṣus: it concerns the greed and accumulation of interest by Upananda.
The householder was unable to repay his debts and wished to extinguish his interest through the power of the Buddha.
He then prepared a meal and invited the Buddha and the Sangha.
Bhadananda made the invitation;
having invited them, he departed elsewhere.
The Buddha and the community of monks arrived at his house first.
Because Khaṇḍa Nanda had not arrived, they did not prepare the offering;
only after Khaṇḍa Nanda had arrived did they serve the food.
Before the meal was even finished, Khaṇḍa Nanda departed first.
The Buddha returned to the vihāra intending to establish the precepts.
At the hour of *prahāṇa*, he assembled the Saṃgha;
only Nanda did not arrive.
When evening arrived, he finally returned.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus,
"The foolish man Pānanda!"
Now, if one causes disturbance to the Saṃgha twice in a single day—
should a bhikṣu, having been invited by another to provide a meal for the Saṃgha,
go to another household before, during, or after the midday meal without having informed them.
If one enters other houses along the way, one commits an offense for each entry;
if one leaves the host's boundary, one commits a *duṣkṛta* for every alley passed through;
if one returns late after having announced [one's arrival], causing distress to the Saṃgha, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For this reason, others need not be requested.
During the time of the Saṃgha, one should announce [the matter] before, at midday, and after;
the meaning of the announcement is as stated above.
When entering a village from one of three locations during improper times,
as well as returning from those three locations,
one must first announce the intention before re-entering the village.
The offenses are all as described above.
(82) A Kṣatriya consecrated great king, until night has not yet dawned and his treasures have not yet been stored away—except for a weighty cause. King Prasenajit had deep faith in the Buddha-dharma.
He caused each of the ladies-in-waiting to invite the Buddha individually to enter the palace and receive the Dharma.
Kāḷodāyin was the teacher of Queen Mallikā.
At one time, early in the morning, he entered the royal palace.
The king had gone out, and the queens had not yet risen;
thus, as he was about to withdraw, he paused.
The precious robes he wore were so light and translucent that they clearly revealed his body;
seeing his teacher, he felt shame and remorse,
and knelt with his right knee on the ground before him.
Kāḷudāyin was also deeply ashamed;
he immediately returned to the midst of the Saṃgha and related the matter in detail.
The Buddha said:
There are two kinds of faults when a bhikṣu enters a royal household;
because of these, the precept was established and he was no longer permitted to enter the households of kṣatriyas.
Brahmins and householders may both become kings.
When a king assumes the throne, he takes water from the four oceans and pours it over his head;
therefore, he is called an "anointed king" (abhiṣikta-rāja).
"Gate-idle" (men-xian) refers to a wooden figure of a person erected before the palace gate.
Regarding "night not yet dawned" (ye-wei-xiao), there are two meanings in the Hu language:
first, that it has not yet dawned.
If the two ladies have not yet risen,
and the king and ladies have not yet departed with the precious robes still unhidden,
and a bhikṣu enters within the threshold of the wooden doorframe, he commits a pāyattika offense.
The king and his consort both brought out precious robes to conceal [the Buddha],
so that there was no offense. Later, the consort of King Udayana wished to invite the Buddha and the Sangha into the palace to provide offerings.
Knowing this, she established a precept that the assembly would certainly not accept.
The various ladies-in-waiting spoke together and exhorted the king,
but the king could not bring himself to comply.
He established a wheel-palace and invited the monks;
outside the palace, he immediately ordered the wheel to move far away,
and the assembly of monks blocked its path of approach.
When the King knew that the Saṃgha had finished eating, he ordered each of his consorts to present their own precious offerings.
Then he said to the Saṃgha,
"Virtuous ones, you may depart."
The assembly said,
"The Buddha has decreed that one must not enter the royal palace.
The king said:
"I shall now instruct you on how to enter the palace.
At that time, the assembly of monks offered prayers of blessing and departed.
Because of this, it was further permitted that those with significant business may enter.
If a king, a queen, a crown prince, or a high-ranking official invites one to enter [a house], there is no offense.
(83) I have now for the first time learned of this matter; it shall be included in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. The bhikṣu Chanda commits a *pāyantika* offense that may be confessed.
The bhikṣus instructed him to repent,
to which he replied:
"Previously, I did not know."
"I have only now come to know this;
I wish not to commit an offense.
However, the various bhikṣus already know and have heard of its number."
If one knows that the offense has been confessed two or three times, yet claims not to know that it has been exceeded,
then this Channa is not exempt from the offense; he does not escape the transgression,
for the offense incurs guilt according to what was actually done.
Furthermore, if one speaks as though knowing something for the first time when one has known it for a long time, one commits an offense;
this is the first of the ninety rules concerning the precept against speaking of what was forgotten.
Furthermore, if one truly does not know, it must be because one was not attentive at the time of listening.
To be inattentive while listening constitutes an offense of transgression (pāyattika).
In this context, the offense is defined precisely by the lack of attentiveness during listening.
If one does not listen attentively when the five categories of precepts (*pañcāpattinikāya*) and the Vinaya-sūtras are being recited,
one commits a *pāyattika* offense for each instance.
If one does not listen attentively when other sūtras or any *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts) are being recited, [one likewise commits an offense].
Each *duṣkṛta* offense:
if ten people present at the *maṇḍala* do not recite the *karmavācanā*, they all commit a *duṣkṛta*.
This is because, in the event of such an error, there is no intention (*saṃjñā*) to perform it correctly.
84. Regarding bone, tooth, or horn needle-cases: when the householder Nādi offered needle-cases and other items to the Saṃgha as he pleased, the monks took them without moderation.
His family was impoverished,
and the people criticized and disparaged him;
consequently, the assembly would not permit it.
"Bones" refers to the bones of elephants and snakes.
"Horns" refers to those of sheep and pigs.
"Tusks" refers to the tusks of elephants and pigs.
"Horns" refers to the horns of oxen, sheep, or deer.
To make a needle case from these materials constitutes an offense of falling (pācittiya),
as it arises from a desire for beauty.
Because it is impure.
Regarding the seven types of objects among the ninety matters, once they have been broken, one must repent in the midst of the Saṃgha.
These cases of broken needle-cases require confession within the Saṃgha after they have been destroyed.
If the saṃgha has not yet been split, one should command that it be split.
If one does not plunder the entire saṃgha, one commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If the command is not obeyed, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If it is returned to the owner and the owner does not accept it,
or if it is given to another, the owner will suffer distress;
to give it to the Sangha would likewise be contrary to the Dharma.
Only disparaging and violating [the rules] is most blameworthy.

Regarding the eighty-fifth rule: the legs of a sitting bed or a reclining bed should be eight finger-breadths high; if they exceed this height, one commits a *pāyattika* offense. Chanda made a bed that was high, wide, and beautiful.
When the Tathāgata was traveling,
he had to look at it himself;
he then rebuked him for that very act.
The Sangha was assembled and the precepts were established.
Since even those who have abandoned the eight precepts [are so affected],
how much more so for a bhikṣu who has abandoned the causes of desire?
There are two kinds of rope beds:
first, those with coarse cords;
second, those with fine cords.
It shall be eight feet long and four feet wide,
with a height of eight finger-breadths of the Buddha.

The Saṃgha should issue a formal command (*ājñā*).

The monks are all without offense. 86.
If one personally uses *tūla* cotton for stuffing or weaving, and another person commits the offense of *pāyattika*, *tūla* is the general name for the down of grasses and trees.

Because it is difficult to obtain,

if it exceeds the limit, it should be cut down.

pus and blood flowed out,

Once the bhikṣus knew they were permitted to possess them,

Whether in length or width,

Later, because Kāḷudāyin’s body was large...
With both knees touching the ground,

add a hand-span to each of the four sides.

He was six cubits wide.

Regarding the matter of not cutting [the robe], the instructions are also as above.
